parties:
Amar Chandra Saha -------- Appellant.
Vs.
Ajit Kumar Das -------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
3. Plaintiff-landlord claimed exclusive ownership of suit premises. He further stated that the original monthly rent was of Tk. 35/- but was subsequently raised to Tk. 37.50 paisa by the House Rent Controller The tenant had stopped payment of rent after Agrahayan 1371 B.S. 

 5. The tenant moved the Dacca High Court in revision challenging the order of ejectment. The revision was heard by a Single Judge of the High Court. The learned Judge found that the tenant-defendant was inducted into the premises by the appellant and his uncle Lakshmi Narayan, and on the latter leaving for India some years ago, the tenant was paying rent to the appellant alone. On the appellant's case that he had become 16 annas owner of the premises on the basis of the family arrangement it was held that such a claim of ownership without a registered deed could not be sustained as no title passed to the appellant. A question was raised before the learned Judge that the tenant-defendant attorned to the appellant as his landlord, but the learned Judge found that the evidence in support of attornment was the payment of rent, and he was of the view that it was not conclusive, though it he was not so stated in the Judgment. The tenant-defendant was not estopped under section 116 of the Evidence Act from denying the appellants title and so he reversed the decision of the trial court and directed the return of the plaint for presentation of the plaint before the proper court for adjudication of all disputes raised in the suit. 

 6. Before dealing with the question under appeal, it should be remembered that the appellant did not succeed in obtaining leave against the other finding of the High Court that by amicable family arrangement the appellant could not claim the vesting of exclusive legal title in him. The appellant has obtained leave, on the footing that the tenant by paying rent to him and depositing rent with the Rent Controller in the sole name of the appellant, has attorned to him as his landlord. The question, therefore, can be divided under two heads. Whether payment of rent in the present case has constituted attornment, and whether by attornment to the appellant, the tenant-defendant is estopped under section 116 of the Evidence Act from denying his exclusive title to the suit premises. 

 7. On the first question it is to be noted that whether payment of rent constitutes attornment or not is a mixed question of law and fact. The High Court has not clearly come to any finding because it took the view that the tenant could challenge the question of derived title of the landlord which occurred after the creation of the tenancy. In the present case the appellant claims derived title by way of family arrangement after the creation of the tenancy. We find no good reason to reverse the view the High Court has taken. The next question is whether attornment attracts the estoppel rule under section 116 of the Evidence Act: 

 8. Attornment means the act of the tenant putting one person in place of another as his landlord. It is well settled that mere payment of rent, or agreement to pay rent in favour of a particular person, without any other evidence, does not always constitute an attornment. There may be various reasons and circumstances for a tenant to pay rent to a person who is not the original landlord. In case of a person claiming derivative title from the original landlord the tenant can always show that the title is not perfect. The language of section 116 of the Evidence Act is clear enough to constitute estoppel between tenant and the landlord at the time of the creation of tenancy. This statutory estoppel, therefore, binds the original contracting parties and at the time of the creation of the tenancy. The section does not estop a tenant from denying the right, as his landlord, of a person who claims to have succeeded to the landlord who put the tenant in possession, or who sues on the basis of a title derived from one who had inducted the tenant in the premises. 

 10. If we turn to the facts of the case under appeal, we find that the appellant in his plaint never set up a case of attornment on payment of rent. It is only when the tenant-defendant in his written statement challenged his exclusive title that, at the time of trial, evidence was led to set up an estoppel, an account of payment of rent by the tenant and his filing of rent deposit case with the Rent Controller in the exclusive name of the appellant. The High Court was not convinced on this evidence, and there is justification for so doing, in view of the fact that the appellant appears to have no exclusive title to the suit premises. His claim is based on the acquisition of title from his uncle Lakshmi Narayan on the basis of a family arrangement, which is not supported by a registered deed. In the face of this plain fact, which again was not asserted in the plaint, but subsequently brought out in evidence, it is manifest that the conclusion of attornment could hardly be drawn from the mere fact of payment of rent by the Tenant.
justice_names: Mr. Justice A. F. M. Ahsanuddin Chowdhury

parties:
Md. Abdul Gafur and another ------- Plaintiff-appellants.
Vs.
Md. Badsha Matbor and others -------- Defendant-respondents.
full_judgment:
Md. Mansur Alam, J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated on 13.11.2014 (decree signed on 20.11.2014) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj in Title Suit No. 92 of 2008. 

 The facts relevant for disposal of this appeal, in brief, are that the plaintiff-respondent filed Title Suit No. 92 of 2008 in the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj, impleading the defendant-appellant for specific performance of contract of a registered agreement deed for sale of 4.50 decimal lands as described in the schedule of the plaint. The scheduled land while owning and possessing by the defendant-appellant, they entered into a contract of sale with the plaintiff respondents for a consideration of Taka 16,74,000/-.Thereafter on 10.05.2007 they executed and registered a baina deed no. 4003 and took taka 10,000/- out of the said value of the land and thereafter they also took taka 70,000/-from the plaintiff-respondent on 27.07.2007 as consideration money but subsequently refused to receive the remaining amount of taka 6,04,000/-from the plaintiff and thereby cause of action arose to file the suit. 

 Defendant-appellants entered in the suit filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending inter alia, that there is no cause of action for filing the suit, that the learned Joint District Judge without considering the facts and circumstances, evidences and the provisions of law most illegally decreed the suit. Admittedly the defendant-appellants entered into a registered agreement for sale with the plaintiff-respondent that the plaintiff-respondent will get the impugned deed as a registered one within a period of 4 (four) months from the date of execution of the agreement for sale dated 07.05.2007 on payment of balance consideration of amount and with further condition that if the plaintiff-respondent 1 failed to take registration of the sale deed on payment of the balance amount within the prescribed period of 4 months, the agreement for sale (bainapatra) will be treated as cancelled. As the plaintiff-respondent failed to take registration on payment of the balance consideration of money within the stipulated period of time the agreement for sale was automatically cancelled as per the terms of the Bainapatra and hence there is no existence of the said agreement after 07.09.2007. As the plaintiff-respondent filed the suit without adhering the terms and condition of the agreement for sale, so he is not entitled to get any relief in this suit. Learned Joint District Judge without considering the terms and condition of the agreement for sale, decreed the suit erroneously. Plaintiff case is bad in law and fact. So the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 6. Whether plaintiff is entitled to get relief as prayed for? 

 The learned trial Judge upon hearing the parties and on considering the evidence and materials on record decreed the suit mainly on the ground that the plaintiff by adducing evidence has been able to prove his contention to the effect that as the defendant-appellant transferred the suit land within the period of existence of the alleged Bainanama, so the said transfer to defendant no.4 is totally illegal and the plaintiff-respondent therefore is entitled to get the relief of specific performance of contract and the plaintiff-respondent complied with all the requirements of the bainanama. 

 On the contrary learned counsel Mr. Mohammad Eunus appearing for the plaintiff-respondent stated that there are mentioning 4 months time limitation of said Baina but the specific date of limitation is not mentioned. So in this circumstances the limitation to file the suit is within 1(one) year from the date of refusal to give registration by the defendant-appellant. Learned counsel for the plaintiff-respondent argues that one of the defendant-appellant took taka 70,000/- from the plaintiff-respondent as consideration on 27.07.2007. This plaintiff-respondent gave notice of the plaintiff-appellant on 11.11.2007 to get the deed registered. Learned counsel further submits that the plaintiff-respondent did not hand over the mutation and subdivision khatian in their favour which the defendant-appellant undertook in the Bainanama. In this way the defendant-appellant has failed to perform their reciprocal promises as they have been assigned to perform. Learned counsel referred the case of Amir Hossain Sowdagor vs Md. Harun-or-Rashid in 65 DLR (AD) at page 130 which is very much applicable in this case. Learned counsel further submits that the provision of section 53B of the Transfer of Property Act expresses that “No immovable property under a contract for sell shall be transferred except to the vendee so long the contract subsists, unless the contract is lawfully rescinded and any transfer made otherwise shall be void. Therefore, the subsequent transfer by the defendant-appellant to the defendant no. 4 on 13.01.2008 is illegal. So as being illegal and void the defendant no. 4 Abdus Salam has no right, title and possession over the suit land. The appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

 On careful perusal of the evidences and materials on record, we find that the plaintiff respondent brought the original Title Suit no. 92 of 2008 praying for the issuance of an order for execution and registration of the kabala deed. Plaintiff- respondent also praying for further order that on failure of the defendant, Court itself would be kind enough to execute and register the kabala deed to this plaintiff on the part of the defendant. 

 The doctrine of bonafide purchaser for value without notice is applicable in a case when the plaintiff wants to enforce the agreement for sale not only against the vendor but also against the transferee of vendor’s title arising subsequent to the plaintiff’s agreement for sale.” 

 The defendant-appellant has been succeeded to discharge his onus adducing oral and documentary evidence. Therefore, we are constrained to hold that the impugned judgment of the learned trial court does not deserve to be sustained. The learned trial judge erred in law and facts as he failed to properly evaluate the evidence on record as to the existence of the impugned bainanama and the possession over the suit land, learned trial judge erroneously concluded that the plaintiff-respondent by adducing evidence proved his case and he is entitled to get the relief of specific performance of contract which is perverse being contrary to the evidence and materials on record. 

 In the result, the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and decree dated 13.11.2024 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj in Title Suit No. 92 of 2008 decreeing the suit is set aside.

parties:
Sheikh Murad Hossain and others ------- Petitioner
vs
A. Gaffar Khan and others --------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2.1 The common facts, relevant for the disposal of the Civil Revisions, in short, are that in execution of Artha decree obtained by Uttara Bank Ltd. Hatkhola Road Branch, Dhaka, (opposite party No.9), the decree holder bank filed Artha Rin Execution Case No. 59 of 1997 before the Fourth Court of Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka against the petitioners in these Civil Revisions. In execution process of the said decree, the Artha Rin Adalat concerned issued notice as regards attachment of the property of the petitioners, which they mortgaged in favour of the Bank to secure the credit facility obtained by them. During such execution process, the opposite party Nos. 1-8 in Civil Revision No. 925 of 2006 and opposite party No. 1 in Civil Revision No. 927 of 2006 filed two sets of applications under Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure for releasing the said properties from such attachment process claiming themselves to be the owners of the said property by way of purchase from the admitted original owner. Accordingly, the said applications were registered as Miscellaneous Case Nos. 27 of 2002 and 28 of 2002. 

 2.2 The common case of the said claimants before the executing Court is that they purchased the said property by way of registered purchase deeds either from the admitted owner, Sheikh Mozahar Ali or from the transferee of the said admitted owner. The said Miscellaneous Cases were contested by the heirs of the said admitted owner, namely the petitioners in these Civil Revisions as opposite parties by filing written objections mainly contending that the admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali did not make any such transfer by way of sale, and that after the death of the said admitted owner, they (the petitioners) remained owners in possession of the said property by way of inheritance, and they muted their names in order to pay khajna etc. Their further case is that at one stage of such ownership and possession, they tried to sell the said property by way of agreement/baina in favour of one Mr Ahmed Ali Chowdhury, who published legal notice in the daily Ittefaq on 29-7-1988. But nobody raised objection about such proposal of sale or such ownership of the petitioners in respect of the land in question. However, the said sale agreement was later cancelled. That the petitioners then mortgaged the said property with the opposite party No.9-Bank on 16-5-1991 in order to obtain some credit facilities, and, accordingly, the Bank filed execution case for execution of the decree obtained against them wherein attachment proceedings commenced in respect of the said property. That the claimants created some forged deeds, and, accordingly, they do not have any right, title, and interest in the said property. The decree holder bank also opposed the said applications filed by the claimants by filing separate written objection, thereby, supporting the case of the petitioners in these Civil Revisions. 

 2.3 In support of the case of the claimants in the said miscellaneous cases, four witnesses were produced. The claimants also produced several documents, which were marked as exhibit Nos. 1-9. On the other hand, the petitioners and the bank produced several documents which were marked as Exhibits 'Ka' to 'Uma' and Exhibit Ka(ka). Thereupon, the Executing Artha Rin Adalat, after hearing the parties, rejected both the Miscellaneous Cases vide orders dated 23-5-2004 taking the view that the claimants or their predecessors in interest purchased the said property from the admitted owner Shekh Mozahar Ali even before creation of interest and title in favour of Mojahar Ali in respect of the said property on the point that the registration in respect of such transfer was not entered in the balam book of the registration office at the time when such transfer took place. According to the executing adalat, although the admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali purchased the said property by registered deed No. 40919, which was executed in his favour on 23-11-1978, the same was recorded in the balam of the Registry Office on 4-11-1981, and, accordingly, during this time in between 23-11-1978 and 4-11-1981, the title of the property did not pass in favour of the said Sheikh Mozahar Ali, and, accordingly, the transfer made by Mozahar Ali was no transfer in the eye of law. 

 2.4 Being aggrieved by such orders and finding of the Artha Rin Executing Adalat, the claimants preferred appeal before the Court of District Judge, Dhaka, being Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 16 of 2004 and 15 of 2004. Accordingly, the said miscellaneous appeals were transferred to the First Court of Additional District Judge, Dhaka for hearing and disposal. Thereupon, the said Court, after hearing the parties, allowed both the appeals vide impugned orders dated 2-11-2005 holding the view that the claimants succeeded in establishing their title in respect of the property in question, and, accordingly, the said properties were not liable to be attached in the said execution case. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and orders, the heirs of the admitted owner, as petitioners, have obtained Rules in the aforesaid Civil Revisions. 

 3.1 Mr Md Ahiya, learned advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the petitioners are the admitted heirs of Sheikh Mozahar Ali. Therefore, the property automatically devolved on them on the admitted death of Mozahar Ali. According to him, the petitioners became owners in possession of the said property by way of inherence. By referring to the impugned judgment and orders, learned advocate submits that the impugned judgments passed by the appellate Court are non-speaking judgments and orders and, by the impugned judgments, the appellate Court has mechanically set-aside the judgment of the Artha Rin Executing Adalat which gave judgment in favour of the petitioners taking the view that the transfer in favour of the said claimants of the disputed property was not lawful transfer and such transfer did not pass any title in favour of the claimants. By referring to another observation of the executing adalat as regards publication of sale notice in the newspaper by the proposed purchaser of the land, learned advocate submits that the executing adalat categorically held that when such notice was published, the claimants did not raise any objection against the same, although the claimants were in possession ai the relevant time. Therefore, according to him, the appellate Court having allowed the appeal without controverting the questions of facts and law decided by the executing adalat in favour of the petitioners, the impugned judgments and orders should be set-aside. 

 3.2 He submits further that the. Miscellaneous Cases filed by the claimants were barred by the proviso to Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code inasmuch as that they intentionally delayed in filing the said Miscellaneous Cases which is apparent from their depositions before the Court below. Therefore, he submits that since the claimants failed to prove their title, possession, and their bonafide interest in claiming the title in the said property or release of the property from attachment at the earlier opportunity, the appellate Court below has committed gross illegality in setting aside the judgment and orders passed by the executing adalat. 

 3.3 As against above submissions, Mr Md Hamidur Ralunan, learned advocate appearing for both sets of opposite parties, submits that the main issue in this case before the executing adalat was as to when the title of the suit property was passed in favour of the purchaser from the admitted owner Mozahar Ali or whether the title was at all passed in their favour. Therefore, he submits that other collateral issues were unnecessarily discussed by the executing adalat in order to justify the rejection of the said miscellaneous cases. 

 3.4 By referring to the provisions under Section 47 of the Registration Act, he submits that the title of admitted owner sheikh Mozahar Ali in the property in question passed in favour of the purchasers of the said property on the day he executed the transfer deed. According to him, registration of a title deed being a legal requirement, such registration strengthens such transfer of title, and it is immaterial as to when the said registration got its entry into the balam book of the registration office concerned. In support of his such submission, he has referred to decisions in Ata Ullah vs Custodian Evacuee Property, 16 DLR (SC) 298 and Messrs. Green & White vs Registrar, IS Companies, 15 DLR 492. 

 3.5 Learned advocate submits that the issue of passing of title from the original admitted owner as decided by the executing adalat is bereft of any legal authority, and, as such, the same should be set-aside immediately even though the said issue has not been categorically addressed by the appellate Court below. By referring to Exhibit-9, namely the inquiry report done by surveyor office, he submits that as per the said inquiry report, the claimants were found in possession of the suit property, but the executing adalat, in a very cursory way, ignored the finding of possession in the said inquiry report. 

 4.1 To address the issues raised by the contesting parties, we have examined the impugned judgment and orders passed by the lower appellate Court. It appears that the said judgment has been delivered not in accordance with law inasmuch as that the said judgment did not address the issues on the basis of which the lower executing adalat decided the dispute concerned. The lower appellate Court discussed nothing about the possession of the respective parties. Most importantly, it did not address the issue of execution of transfer deed or as to when the title passes upon such execution and the effect of registration of transfer deed in respect of immovable properties as provided by the relevant provisions of the Registration Act. 

 4.2 The same mistake, although in similar way, has been done by the executing adalat inasmuch as that it took the view (rightly or wrongly) that the title did not pass at the time of execution of the transfer deed by the admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali on the ground that the registered deeds did not get their place in the balam book of the registration office. However, frustratingly, the lower executing adalat did not cite any authority or law on the basis of which it reached such conclusion, particularly when there are specific provisions of law in this regard as provided by Transfer of Property Act and Registration Act. Therefore, we have no option but to discuss the core issues of this case, namely, as to when the title passed from the admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali in favour of the purchasers by the said deeds. 

 4.3 As per the claim of the claimants, the admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali became owner in possession of the said property by way of purchase from the admitted transferor Radha Bhallav Mandal, who executed such transfer deed on 23-11-1978 (Exhibit-Ka), which, according to the executing adalat, got its entry in the balam book of the registration office on 4-11-1981. The question raised before the executing adalat was whether the title in the property passed in favour of Sheikh Mozahar Ali on the date of execution and registration of the said transfer deed, namely, on 23-11-1978. In this regard, we may refer to the provisions under Section 8 of the Transfer of Property Act which provides that a transfer takes place forthwith unless a different intention is expressed, or necessarily implied, and such transfer passes forthwith to the transferee all the interest which the transferor is then capable of passing in the property and all the legal incidents thereof. 

 4.4 It was not the case of the petitioners before the executing adalat that the said transfer deed, by which the admitted owner got title, was a forged transfer deed. The very title of the petitioners before the executing adalat also is based on the said transfer deed by Radha Ballav in favour of Sheikh Mozahar Ali. Therefore, it appears from the judgment of the executing adalat that the whole issue circled around the effect of execution of transfer deed and/or registration thereof. 

 4.5 As stated above, a transfer of immovable property passes forthwith all the title, interest in the transferor in favour of the transferee as per the provisions of Section 8 of the Transfer of Property Act. Now, the requirement of registration of such transfer deed is requirement of law in order to safeguard such transfer from any future question, and by such registration, the State becomes party to such transfer, and the Legislature has given a kind of protection in favour of such registered transfer by operation of law in that it gets presumption of correctness once it is registered, unless contrary is proved. Section 47 of the Registration Act is very much clear in this regard which provides that a registered document shall operate from the time which it would have commenced to operate, if no registration thereof had been required or made and not from the time of its registration. Therefore, the Legislature has made it clear that since the registration of a transfer deed is a formal requirement, the transfer in fact started to operate at the time when such transfer is made by way of execution of transfer deeds although, at that point of time, the said deed was not registered formally. Now, the Legislature has subsequently made such transfer mandatory even by saying that any transfer without such registration will be void. This statutory requirement of registration of transfer deed in respect of immovable property has been provided only to safeguard the transferor and the transferee from any manipulation or subsequent fraudulent act in respect of such transfer, as because the State becomes witness to such transfer by way of such registration. 

 4.6 Again, the further formalities as regards certification of such registration and/or endorsement of such registration, as provided by Part X of the Registration Act are also formalities to be complied with by registration office upon such registration of a transfer deed in respect of immovable property. The transferor or transferee has got nothing to do with that. Therefore, it cannot be said that even if a registration is not certified or any delay takes place in the certification of such transfer or entry of such transfer in the balam book of the registration office, the transfer did not take place. On this point, it appears, the executing adalat has committed gross mistake of law, which is apparent from the judgment of the executing adalat. Based on that misconceived idea of law of transfer and registration, the executing adalat proceeded to the extent of holding the view that the admitted owner Mozahar Ali did not get any title in respect of the said property before 4-11-1981, when the said registration as regard his purchase was recorded in the balam book of the registration office. From this misconceived idea, the executing adalat held that the title in respect of the said property did not pass in favour of the said Sheikh Mozahar Ali before 4-11-1981. This view of the executing adalat does not have any basis of law. Rather, it is clearly contrary to the provisions of law as stated above. The subsequent observations of the executing adalat were nothing but to justify his main legal contention as regards transfer of title in favour of the original owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali, particularly, when it is apparent that the executing adalat clearly ignored Exhibit-9 without assigning any reason, wherein the inquiry of the surveyor office found the claimants' possession in the disputed land. This being the position of law and fact, we do not need to deliberate on other collateral issues, which are not very relevant for determining the main issue of transfer of the title. The other contention of the petitioners before the executing adalat as regards the signature of admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali on the transfer deed, by which Mozahar Ali transferred the property in favour of the claimants, also could not be established by them. 

 4.7 The executing adalat did not even consider that point by assigning reason in the judgment delivered by it. Therefore, since the registered title deeds, by which the claimants purchased disputed properties, namely, Exhibit-2, 3, 5, being registered transferred deeds, they have legal protection in their favour and such protection cannot be taken away by mere statements of anybody that the said documents were false documents, unless the party claiming the same be false adduces sufficient evidence, which is clearly absent in this case. 

 4.8 Therefore, we are of the view that the claimants in the miscellaneous cases concerned have been able to establish their title in respect of the disputed property, and, accordingly, the executing adalat should have released the said property from the clutches of attachment in view of the provisions under Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

parties:
Gulap Rahman ---------- Petitioner
VS
Dr. ATM Gulam Kabir and others ---------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
In this Civil Revision, the Rule was issued calling upon opposite party Nos.1-10 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 11-11-2010 (decree signed on 21-12-2010) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Noakhali in Title Appeal No.84 of 2000, affirming the judgment and decree dated 15-3-2000 (decree signed on 27-3-2000) passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Noakhali in Title Suit No.53 of 1984, decreeing the suit should not be set-aside and/or why such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper, shall not be passed. 

 Pending the hearing of the Rule, the operation of the judgment and decree dated 11-11-2010 passed in the said Title Appeal No.84 of 2000 was stayed initially for 6(six) months. The period of stay was subsequently extended from time to time. 

 2. One Robindra Kumar Ghosh as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.53 of 1984 in the Court of learned Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Noakhali for a declaration that the Kabala Deed Nos.21203, 21204, 21205, and 21206 all were executed on 6-10-1978 and registered on 7-10-1978 purportedly executed by Robindra Kumar Ghosh in favour of Mst. Ozifa Khatun is forged, fraudulent, without any consideration, false, collusive, ineffective, and not binding upon the plaintiff as well as upon the suit property. 

 3. The plaintiff's case, in short, is that the original plaintiff Robindra Kumar Ghosh got some properties from his father Deb Chandra Ghosh by a registered deed of gift dated 10-4-1976. Then, he sold 2.18 acres of land to the defendant Nos.2-8 by different sale deeds. While Robindra Kumar Ghosh and defendant Nos.2-8 were in possession of their respective land, they came to know that having falsely personated a man as Robindra Kumar Ghosh got 4(four) kabala deeds registered bearing Nos. 21203, 21204, 21205 and 21206 all dated 7-10-1978 in favour of defendant No.1. But Robindra Kumar Ghosh never executed such sale deeds. He did not know about it and those kabala deeds were created by forgery. He did not put any thumb impression or signature in any such deed, nor did he execute and register the same upon appearing in person before the Sub-Registrar but, defendant No.1 got the said forged deed executed and registered by falsely personating any of her man as Robindra Kumar Ghosh. Even, he did not receive any consideration from defendant No. 1. Thus, defendant No.1 was never in possession of the suit land. At that time, Robindra Kumar Ghosh had no necessity for selling or intention to sell the suit property. But the unruly sons of defendant No.1 being greedy for others' properties created those forged documents in favour of their mother, defendant No.1. Initially, Robindra Kumar Ghosh came to know about the said forged deeds at the last part of the month of Chaitra, 1390 BS and exactly he came to know about the same on 24-4-1984 and 25.04.1984 and upon obtaining certified copy thereof and, as such, that very Robindra Kumar Ghosh as plaintiff instituted the suit. 

 4. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations brought by the plaintiff and contending, inter alia, that in the need of cash, Robindra Kumar Ghosh proposed to sell the suit property and the defendants accepted the proposal. Upon negotiation, the consideration money was fixed at Taka 72,000. Accordingly, four deeds all dated 6-10-1978 were executed by Robindra Kumar Ghosh upon receiving the entire consideration money in the presence of the witnesses and the same were registered on 7-10-1978 while one Shafiullah identified him before the Sub-Registrar. Thus, all four deeds are genuine and those were executed and registered upon receiving the consideration money by Robindra Kumar Ghosh himself. Accordingly, he also made delivery of possession except for a part of his homestead wherein he had been living with the promise that he would go elsewhere. But Robindra Kumar Ghosh subsequently might have created several deeds in favour of defendant Nos.2-8. But he never disclosed the same to defendant No.1 while defendant Nos. 2-8 are not in possession in any part of the suit land. Thus, the said deeds have not been acted upon. It is not true that the four sons of defendant No.1, Mostafa Miah, Golap Rahman, Shahjahan and Nazim Uddin created the forged deed. Accordingly, the plaintiff filed the false suit only to cause damage to defendant No. 1. Thus, the plaintiff having no right, title or possession of the suit property, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 9. Against the judgment and decree of the Trial Court, defendant Nos.1(ka)-1(uma) preferred Title Appeal No.84 of 2000 before the Court of the learned District Judge, Noakhali and the appeal was transferred to the 2nd Court of Additional District Judge, Noakhali for its disposal. The Court of Appeal below upon hearing both the parties by the judgment and decree dated 11-11-2010 (decree signed on 21-12-2010) dismissed the appeal. 

 11. Having placed the Civil Revision, Mr Shasti Sarker along with Mr Md Abdur Rashid, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that both the Courts below failed to consider that upon execution and registration of the deeds in question, the plaintiff himself delivered the possession of the suit property and they have still been in possession and thus, the sale deeds have been acted upon. Both the Courts below also failed to consider that the subsequent purchasers had no legal right and authority to continue the suit on behalf of the sole deceased plaintiff. Again, both the Courts below failed to consider that the thumb impressions and signatures of the deceased plaintiff as appeared in the volume book were not compared with those in the admitted documents. Moreover, neither the thumb impression expert nor the handwriting expert properly conducted their respective examination and therefore, the reports submitted and the opinion made by them being not in accordance with the law, the suit should be sent on remand for trial afresh specially, for examination of the thumb impression and signatures of the original plaintiff as appeared in the volume books by comparing the same with any admitted thumb impressions or signatures of that very deceased plaintiff the learned Advocate further submits that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner as therein it has not been prayed for setting aside the sale deeds in question as required by section 39 of the Specific Relief Act. 

 12. On the other hand, Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury, learned Advocate for opposite party Nos.l-5 and 7-10 submits that both the Courts below concurrently found that the kabala deeds in question are forged documents upon considering the report as well as the depositions of the thumb impression expert and the handwriting expert. Against the application for sending five registered deeds executed by the original plaintiff for comparing the thumb impressions and signatures of the original plaintiff therein with the purported thumb impressions and signatures of the original plaintiff that appeared in the respective volume books, defendant No.1 or her heirs did not raise any objection and in the written objection against the report of the handwriting expert, they have also not raised any objection as to the admitted thumb impressions and the signatures of the original plaintiff and in the written objection against the report of the thumb impression expert, they stated in a contradictory way, once stating that those were not properly compared then, said that those were not even admitted thumb impression but, the said objections were rejected. Against the said rejection, the defendants did not take any step, nor even had they taken any ground in the Memo of Appeal and thus, they have conceded the said order of rejection. Accordingly, both the Courts below rightly made their findings and observations on the said reports and depositions of the thumb impression expert and the handwriting expert. The opposite parties who are the purchasers of the suit property were made assignees of the original plaintiff as they got six sale deeds executed in their favour and then all those deeds were registered upon identification of thumb impression and signatures therein by his two sons inasmuch as in all such deeds, the wife of the original plaintiff and his neighbouring people in the same homestead were also witnesses to the execution of the said six sale deeds. Against the order allowing the applications for appointment of assignees of the original plaintiff though, the defendants filed a written objection, they were not aggrieved by the order passed by the Trial Court. Accordingly, the purchaser plaintiffs were continuing the suit without any subsequent objection as well as based on the order of the learned Trial Court. Moreover, since admittedly the subsequent plaintiffs are the purchasers of the suit land from the original plaintiff thereby, their right, title and interest were created by those sale deeds and as per law, during the lifetime of the original plaintiff, they were entitled to be assignees of the original plaintiff as per Order XXII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure and accordingly, there being no merit in the Rule, the same should be discharged with cost. The learned Advocate further submits that since both the Courts below concurrently found that the four kabala deeds in question are forged documents but, they have used the same as genuine before the Courts below as well as before this Court, a proceeding should be drawn against them under section 476 read with section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 14. As per the plaintiffs' case, Robindra Kumar Ghosh never executed and registered any sale deed in favour of the original defendant No.1 nor even, he received any consideration money from her and accordingly, he also did not make the delivery of possession of the suit property. On the other hand, it is the case of the original defendant No.1 that Robindra Kumar Ghosh himself executed all four deeds and got the same registered upon appearing before the concerned Sub-Registrar and in furtherance thereof, he also made delivery of possession of the suit property upon receiving the consideration money hi the presence of the witnesses. 

 19. In the present case, it appears from both reports that the respective experts came to their conclusion upon examining at least five points. Thus, I do not find any legal infirmity in examining the thumb impressions and signatures of Rabindra Kumar Ghosh by the thumb impression expert as well as by the handwriting expert. Accordingly, upon considering the deposition of Robindra Kumar Ghosh and those of other witnesses including the handwriting expert and thumb impression expert, both the Courts below concurrently held that the sale deeds purportedly executed and registered by Robindra Kumar Ghosh in favour of the original defendant No.1 who was substituted by her four sons and one daughter are forged documents. 

 21. It also appears that the original defendant No.1 died leaving behind four sons and one daughter and they were substituted in the Trial Court. They have also jointly preferred the appeal but only the petitioner alone filed the instant Civil Revision. Thus, from the conduct of other appellants, it appears that they have conceded the judgment and decree of the Courts below. Had there been any merit in their case, they might have filed the instant Civil Revision along with the sole petitioner. Thus, even the circumstantial evidence does not support that the defendant-appellant-petitioner is alone in the possession of the suit property. 

 24. It is the specific case of the plaintiff that four sons of defendant No.1 created the disputed sale deeds by forging the thumb impressions and signatures of the original plaintiff and upon trial both the Courts below concurrently found substance in the case of the plaintiff. Upon considering the material evidence on record, I have also no hesitation to conclude that the original defendant No.1 and her heirs are the beneficiaries of those forged documents and, as such, they themselves in collusion with each other have or caused to have created and registered those sale deeds by forging the signatures and thumb impressions of Robindra Kumar Ghosh upon falsely personating him with intent to cause damage and injury to the original plaintiff as well as his successors-in-interest, to support a title in the suit property, to cause the original plaintiff or his successor-in-interest to part with the suit property and thereby have made valuable securities in respect of the suit property, and fraudulently possessed and used the same as genuine documents as well as corruptly used as true or genuine evidence in this suit before all three Courts, including this Court and thereby prima facie have committed offences under section 93/196/205/463/465/467/471/474/109 of the Penal Code, 1860.

parties:
City Bank Limited, Kushtia Branch, Kushtia ----- Petitioner
VS
Court of First Joint District Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Kushtia and another -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
The petitioner—City Bank Ltd. instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 2 of 2008 before the Court of Joint District Judge, 1st Court and Artha Rin Adalat, Kushtia, the respondent No. 1, shortly called the Adalat, against the respondent No. 2 for realization of outstanding dues to the tune of Taka 5,20,370.62 and interest thereon. Having received the summons, the respondents entered appearance in the suit and contested the same denying the material averments set out in the plaint. After conclusion of the trial, the Adalat was pleased to pass a decree to the suit by its judgment and decree dated 15-6-2008. Accordingly, the decree was drawn and signed on 22-6-2008. Thereafter, the decree holder-Bank put the decree into execution by filing Artha Rin Execution Case No. 06 of 2008 and a notice was floated for selling out the mortgage property on auction but no auction was held. Thereafter, on the prayer of the decree holder-Bank, the Executing Court issued a certificate of ownership or title in respect of mortgage property under section 33(7) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, hereinafter shortly referred to the Ain, 2003. Then the Executing Court sent the copy of the certificate of title for registration and accordingly, the same was registered. After that the Executing Court by its order No. 13, dated 8-7-2009 disposed of the execution case in view of section 33(9) of the Ain, 2003. On 18-3-2013, the judgment-debtor filed an application to get back the property by depositing the outstanding dues of the decretal amount and the application was resisted by the decree holder-Bank. Upon hearing, the Executing Court was pleased to allow the petition filed under section 57 of the Ain, 2003 with some conditions stipulated in the operative portion of the impugned order. Challenging the legality and propriety of the said order, the petitioner-decree holder-Bank moved this Court and obtained the Rule and stay therewith. 

 5. He also contends that since the petitioner-Bank acquired title in the mortgage property in accordance with law, therefore, such right cannot be taken away without due process of law and handing over of possession of the mortgage property is not pre-condition for conferring title therein. 

 i. Was the certificate of title or ownership under section 33(7) of the Ain, 2003 legally issued in the Artha Rin Execution Case No. 06 of 2008? 

 ii. Was the Artha Rin Execution Case No. 06 of 2008 duly disposed of after issuance of certificate of title under section 33(7) of the Ain, 2003? 

 18. On meaningful reading of sub-sections (5), (7), (7Ka) and (7Kha) of section 33 of the Ain, 2003, it transpires that where the possession of property requires to be obtained through intervention of the Court, the decree holder has to file an application in writing to the Executing Court to hand over possession of the said property to the decree holder or the auction purchaser as the case may be and before handing over possession of the property, the Executing Court shall be reassured that it is the property which was lawfully mortgaged by its original owner against the loan liabilities or which was attached under the original title and possession of the judgment-debtor for execution of the decree. The provisions of sub-sections 7Ka and 7Kha of section 33 of the Ain, 2003 were incorporated by the Artha Rin Adalat Ain (Amendment) Act, 2010 (Act XVI of 2010) in order to protect the property of the actual owner. In this case, admittedly, the possession of the mortgage property remains with the judgment-debtor. If the execution case is disposed of upon issuance of certificate of title, the decree holder will not be able to obtain the possession without the intervention of the Court. Therefore, the contention of the petitioner is that upon issuance of certificate of title under section 33(7) of the Ain, 2003, the Executing Court has become f1nctus officio is fallacious and not based on cogent reasons. We may take a look at the other part of the coin, if possession remains with the decree holder, then upon issuance of certificate under sections 33(5) or 33(7) the Executing Court may dispose of the Artha Rin Execution Case by invoking section 33(9) of the Ain, 2003 subject to the provision of section 28 of the Ain, 2003. 

 It appears that the decree-holder appellant filed an application praying for an Order to put the decree-holder into possession of the concerned property as it was allegedly obstructed by the judgment-debtor but the learned Judge, Artha Rin Court, dismissed the petition on the ground that on the issuance of the certificate of title in favour of the decree-holder, the execution case had already been disposed of and the Court has got nothing further to do in this respect. With respect, we are unable to agree with the said views of the learned Judge, Artha Rin Court. Sub-Section 7 envisages vesting of ownership of the property of the judgment-debtor upon the decree-holder. The said vesting of ownership includes delivery of possession of the property. Without the delivery of possession, the execution case cannot be disposed of. 

 ii. In case of issuance of certificate under section 33(5) of the Ain, 2003, it is obligatory to exhaust the auction process under sub-sections (1) and (4) of section 33 of the Ain, 2003. If the certificate of title is issued upon without exhausting the procedure of section 33(4) of the Ain, 2003 that will make the said provision useless and nugatory. In such a case, the Bank or Financial Institutions by a show up auction process under section 33(1) of the Ain, 2003 will straight apply for a certificate of title with an ulterior motive depriving the judgment-debtor from obtaining the actual market price of the property. So we hold the view that before issuance of certificate of title to the mortgage property or other property of the judgment-debtor, the Executing Court shall follow the provisions of sections 33(1) and 33(4) of the Ain, 2003 and after that it will fix the actual market price of the mortgage property or other property and succinctly be stated in the certificate of title so that the outstanding dues if any may be adjusted later on. In such a case, the Executing Court shall determine the actual market price of the mortgage property on the basis of a report from the Sub-Registrar of the local jurisdiction. Apart from the same, in certificate issuing order, the Executing Court shall state as to whether the decretal amount has been adjusted wholly, if not, the amount of outstanding dues should state therein. It repeatedly comes to our notice that the Executing Court mechanically allows the prayer of issuance of certificate of title. Mechanical issue of certificate of title is deprecated by this Court. 

 vi. Section 33(9) of the Ain, 2003 provides that when the rights of possession and use of any property under sub-section (5) or the title of any property under sub-section (7) vests in favour of the decree holder, the suit for execution of the said decree shall, subject to the provisions of section 28, be finally disposed of. The word 'final' is not absolute. It has to be read with sections 28, 33(71(a) and 33(7Kha) of the latest amended Ain, 2010. Therefore, we strongly hold the view that mere issuance of certificate under sections 33(5) and 33(7) of the Ain, 2003 is not enough to finally dispose of the execution case. If the possession of the mortgage property or other property attached by the Executing Court for realizing outstanding loan money remains with the decree holder, the Executing Court may dispose of the execution case in view of section 33(9) of the Ain, 2003. Resorting to literal meaning of section 33(9) of the Ain, 2003 will be a great concern and it may cause devastating consequence, therefore, harmonious construction of the aforesaid provisions is sine qua non to fulfill the purpose of the legislature. 

 vii. As per the mandate of section 58 of the Ain, 2003, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules to give effect to the provisions of this Ain, 2003. Some provisions of the Ain, 2003, need more clarification and to give effect to the provisions therein for the smooth functioning of the Artha Rin Adalat. The Government may formulate comprehensive delegated legislations and the necessary forms like issuance of certificate of title, certificate of possession, enjoyment of usufructs and sale of the mortgage property etc. should be prescribed therein to do away with the confusions crept in the Ain, 2003. 

 xi. Title is legal ownership. Possession is physical control of the movable or immovable property. Possession is the prima facie evidence of ownership, called as nine out of ten points of law meaning that there is a presumption the possessor of a property or thing is owner of it and the other elements in order to have that property or thing must prove their title or better possessory right. Certificate of owner-ship or title equivalent to title deed. Title deed having no possession is only a paper transaction. Title deed is not acted upon unless possession is handed over to the title holder.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Abu Taher Md. Saifur Rahman

caseno:
Civil Revision No. 2705 of 2009
With 
Civil Revision No.2706 of 2009
parties:
Md. Abul Kalam Azad ------ Plaintiff-Respondent-Petitioner
-Vs-
Md. Majibur Rahman and others ------ Defendant-Appellant-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Soumendra Sarker, J.:- The Rule issued calling upon the Opposite Parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 16.06.2009 and 22.06.2009 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur in allowing the Title Appeal No.33 of 2006 along with Title Appeal No.40 of 2006 analogously and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 30.03.2006 and 09.04.2006 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Chandpur in decreeing the Title Suit No.14 of 2001 should not be set aside and/or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present petitioner as plaintiff instituted the original Title Suit being No.14 of 2001 in the 2nd Court of learned Joint District Judge, Chandpur against the defendants for a decree of specific performance of contract in respect of the suit property contending inter alia that the suit property originally belonged to the defendant Narayan Proshad Mondol, who proposed the plaintiff to buy the property and the plaintiff agreed to purchase the same. Accordingly, on 15.05.1984 the consideration amount of the land was fixed at Tk.3,75,000/- and it was settled that on 27.05.1984 out of the total consideration amount, Tk. 3,60,000/- will be paid by the plaintiff for getting a deed of agreement. Accordingly, the plaintiff by the date fixed paid Tk.3,60,000 in favour of the defendant and accordingly the defendant after taking the amount, executed a deed of agreement in favour of the plaintiff and handover possession of the suit property. It was agreed by the parties that after payment of the rest amount of Tk.15,000/- the plaintiff will obtain the sub-kabala deed from the defendant. Thereafter; the plaintiff on several occasions going before the defendant requested him to take the remaining money of consideration and execute and register the sub-kabala deed, but the defendant showing different excuse requested the plaintiff to wait. Last of all, on 05.02.2001 the plaintiff accompanied by his witnesses went to the residence of the defendant to pay the remaining amount of Tk.15,000/-, at which; the defendant told the plaintiff to come on 14.02.2001 at Hajiganj with an undertaking that on the following day he will execute and register a sub-kabala deed in the concerned registry office. But on the date fixed the defendant did not go there, and finding no other alternative the plaintiff instituted the original suit for specific performance of contract. 

 5. In the original suit, the government of Bangladesh, who was the defendant No. 2 contested the suit and the case of the defendant No.2 is such that the original owners of the suit property migrated to India and as such the property has become vested and non-resident property under the government. 

 6. The learned trial court during trial of the original suit after taking evidence from the sides of the respective parties decreed the suit on contest by its judgment and decree .dated 30.03.2006. 

 7. Being aggrieved the defendant No.1 filed Title Appeal No.33 of 2006 and the defendants No. 3-8 filed Title Appeal No. 40 of 2006 in the court of learned District Judge, Chandpur which were transmitted to the Court of learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur for hearing and disposal and the learned appellate court taking analogous hearing of both the two appeals, allowed the same and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court by the impugned judgment and decree dated 16.06.2009. 

 10. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned appellate court during disposal of the appeals committed gross illegality and, irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur committed error of law in allowing the appeals without controverting the findings of the trial court according to the provisions of Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate also submits that the learned Appellate Court gave perverse findings that it is admitted by the seller that he had already transferred his entire share to the 3rd party before the alleged contract for sale. The learned counsel submits that the executant of the contract, did not willfully gave evidence before the court and in the pretext of his false illness that he is dumb and deaf he did not appear before the trial Court, and in this context the learned trial court in his observation and findings in the order sheet clearly opined that the defendant No.1 is a physically sound person and capable of giving evidence but the learned Appellate Court failed to consider that material facts on record, and thereby committed gross illegality resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and that the defendant No.1 has played a foul play in the court, which is against the principle of equity and justice. The learned Advocate also submits that a suit for specific performance of contract is an equitable relief, which is guided by the principle of equity, but the learned Additional District Judge has totally failed to appreciate the actual proposition of law and arrived at an erroneous decision as to the merit of the appeals. The learned Advocate argued that the cause of action of the suit arose on 15.02.2001, when the defendant No.1 by his conduct and dealing expressed his denial to execute and register the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff, and from that date the original suit was filed within time. The learned Advocate also argued that the learned Appellate Court surprisingly made a comment in the impugned judgment and decree that the papers in which the deed of agreement was written are anti-dated, but in fact; the papers in which the deed of agreement was written were not anti-dated and manipulated, rather; the defendant No.1 to the original suit at his free consent and will; executed the same as a "bainanama " in favour of the plaintiff and that the possession was also delivered much earlier and the plaintiff after taking possession over the suit property started to reside therein and that the order-sheets of the trial court; makes it clear that the conduct of the defendant No.1 is not at all satisfactory; rather he has played a foul play with the court. The learned Advocate during his argument argued that the defendant No.1 who was the admitted owner of the suit property categorically admitted his signature in the deed of agreement and as a result; the onus of proof on fraud is entirely lies upon the defendants that the deed of agreement is not genuine; but the defendants have hopelessly failed to discharge their onus of proof by any tangible evidence. The learned counsel for the petitioner submits that vis-à-vis, the plaintiff to the suit to substantiate his claim examined 04 witnesses, who have successfully proved the case of the plaintiff and that the executant of the deed of agreement alleged that he had no title and possession over the suit land and the possession was handed over to the defendants No.3-8, but the 'sole-decree' of Title Suit No. 367 of 1967 speaks that the suit land belonged to the defendant No.1 not to the defendants No.3-8. The learned Advocate lastly submits that without setting aside the aforesaid decree the defendants No.3-8 are debarred from challenging the case of the plaintiff that the defendant No.1 being the owner of the suit land transferred the same in favour of the plaintiff by dint of a deed of agreement. In the 'sole-decree' 2.55 acres of land goes in favour of the defendant No.1 Narayan Chandra and the witness No.2 of the defendant admits that the 'sole-decree' was given on 06.03.1968 and in respect of the kabala deeds of the defendants No.3-8 vide Exhibit-`Ga' series, not a single competent witness have been examined and the learned trial court in his observation and findings adverting evidence on records rightly decided all the issues in favour of the plaintiff. But the appellate court without reversing the findings of the trial court adverting evidence therein, reversed the judgment of the trial court arbitrarily, which is violative to the provision laid down in Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 11. As against the aforesaid submission, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the opposite party opposing the Rule submits that the appellate court during disposal of the appeals committed no illegality or irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that the suit as instituted by the plaintiff was time barred and there is no satisfactory explanation or reason from the side of the plaintiff as to why he kept his silence after 1984. In the year 2001 after a long lapse of time the suit was filed which was highly doubtful. The learned Advocate also submits that after 17 years the suit was filed on false allegations on the basis of a forged deed of agreement and the Appellate Court rightly relied upon the maxim of specific performance of contract that 'delay defeats equity'. The learned Advocate further submits that in the binanama there is no specification of the land and in page No.3 of the bainanama there is a mention of the year 2001, which is the crack of the case. The learned appellate court rightly disbelieved the bainanama of the year 1984 which is a forged document and on the basis of a forged document the plaintiff is not entitled a decree for specific performance of contract. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the defendant No.1 had no title and interest over the suit land and the contract as alleged from the side of the plaintiff bears no value in the eye of law and inasmuch as the plaintiff is not coming in clean hands, he is not entitled to get the decree as prayed for. The learned appellate court after thorough evaluation of the evidence on record rightly decided the merit of the appeals in favour of the appellants and allowed both the two appeals in favour of the defendants and there is no infirmity or misreading and non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with. 

 12. In order to appreciate the submission of the learned Advocates, having gone through the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.14 of 2001 and the Title Appeal No.33 of 2006 along with 40 of 2006 as well as the evidence led from the sides of the respective parties with all other connected papers and the case records it transpires that it is the positive contention of the plaintiff in his pleading that the defendant No.1 being the owner of the suit property described in the schedule of the plaint entered into a deed of agreement in respect of transfer of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff by virtue of a deed of agreement and it was the contract between the parties that, out of the total consideration amount of Tk.3,75,000/-, Tk.3,60,000/- will be paid by 27.05.1984 and the plaintiff to the suit by the date fixed paid the amount and accordingly a deed of agreement was executed by the defendant No.1 in his favour followed by delivery of possession of the suit property. 

 13. On perusal of the plaint as well as the connected documents I find that the corresponding S.A. khatians No.221, 223, 419 and 467 were prepared in the name of one Monindra Chandra and Narayan Chandra Mondal. The contract between the parties was held on 15.05.1984 and the consideration amount was fixed at Tk.3,75,000/-. It is further contention of the plaintiff that on several occasions he went before the defendant No.1 and requested him to execute and register a sale deed in his favour after taking the remaining sum of Tk.15,000/- and lastly on 05.02.2001 when the plaintiff went to the owner Narayan, it was decided between them that on 14.02.2001 the defendant No.1 coming to the concern Hajiganj police station from his residence of Tongibari police station under Munshiganj District, taking the remaining amount of consideration will execute and register a sub-kabala deed on the following day i.e. 15.02.2001, but while the defendant did not appear according to their agreement, the plaintiff finding no other alternative instituted the original suit on 02.04.2001. It further appears from the schedule of the plaint that the land included within the deed of agreement has been specified in the schedule. In the case records it is noticed that the attorney of the defendant No.1 at first filed a written statement in which he has admitted the deed of agreement between the parties in respect of transfer of the suit land by the defendant No.1 in favour of the plaintiff. The 2nd written statement which was filed by the son of the defendant No.1 after cancellation of the power of attorney goes to show that the deed of agreement has been challenged by the subsequent attorney viz. the son (D.W.1) of the defendant No. 1. 

 18. On the other hand; from the side of the defendants, D.W.1 Biswanath Mondal is the son of Narayan Chandra Mondal, who on the basis of a power of attorney from his father deposed before the trial court. During his examination-in-chief he has corroborated his written statement which was filed for the 2nd time by himself. This witness testified at a stage that his father Narayan Chandra gave a power of attorney in favour of Jitu Mia who submitted the lg written statement in the original suit. Subsequently; that power of attorney was cancelled by his father by deed No.642 dated 11.10.2001. 

 19. D.W.2 is Md. Mizanur Rahman Patwary, who is the defendant No.4. This witness testified in his deposition that his father purchased the land from the defendant No.1. This witness further testified in his examination-in-chief that the defendant No.1 had no title, interest in the suit land at the time of deed of agreement. 

 22. In the original suit, one formal witness who is a `mohorar' of Comilla Sadar Joint Sub-registry office deposed as P.W.5, who is Anil Chandra Biswas. This witness testified that he has brought the volume book No.30 and in this book there is an entry of deed No.3186, but there is no consistency with the contents of this deed with the alleged certified copy, which is mentioned in page No.45-48 of the volume book with the certified copies of the same, but in volume book No.6, the certified copy of deed No.877 is consistent with the entry and the contents of deed No.557 of the certified copy is not consistent with the volume book and the certified copy of deed No.5142 is also not consistent with the volume book. Lastly; in comparison with the volume book No.41 the P.W.5 testifies that, there is no consistency of deed No.5127 which is produced as certified copy from the side of the defendants with the concerned volume book. This witness was not cross-examined from the side of the defendants. 

 25. Under the purview of section 12 of the Specific Relief Act (I of 1877) in a suit for specific performance of contract relating to immovable property, time is not the essence of the contract, nor hardship of the defendant is a ground to refuse relief Our lordships in the case of Anwara Begum Md. Karimul Haque and others 5 BLC (AD)119 held that, the point of limitation is not at all the essence of the suit for specific performance of contract. Besides this; when a vendor executes' a deed of sale but it remains unregistered and the vendee sues for specific performance of the original contract, the question is to be considered whether there is a subsisting contract for sale or not and if the contract be subsisting, the vendee has a statutory right to have the contract performed. 

 31. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree dated 16.06.2009 and 22.06.2009 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur in allowing the Title Appeal No.33 of 2006 along with Title Appeal No.40 of 2006 analogously and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 30.03.2006 and 09.04.2006 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Chandpur in decreeing the Title Suit No.14 of 2001 is hereby set aside. 

 32. The judgment and order will govern both the two appeals being Title Appeal No.33 of 2006 and Title Appeal No.40 of 2006 simultaneously.

caseno: First Appeal No. 71 of 2003 with Civil Rule No. 310(f) of 2003.
parties:
MASHRIQUI JUTE MILLS LIMITED 
Vs. 
JIBON BIMA CORPORATION AND OTHERS
full_judgment:
S. H. Md. Nurul Huda Jaigirdar, J: This First Appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 10.07.2002 and 16.07.2002 respectively passed by the Joint District Judge and Commercial Court No.2 Dhaka in Title Suit No. 197 of 2001 decreeing the suit on contest against the defendant appellant and others. 

 2. The suit was filed on 29.10.1988 in the Court of Joint District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka, for sale of the mortgaged properties of defendant No.1 for realization of loan money. The suit eventually was transferred to the Court of Joint District Judge and Commercial Court No.2, Dhaka, and renumbered as Title Suit No.197 of 2001. 

 3. The plaint case, precisely, is that plaintiff is an Insurance Corporation and defendant No.1, herein appellant, is a private limited company; defendant Nos. 2 to 5, are the directors of the defendant No.1; defendant No. 1 obtained foreign currency loan facilities from the then `Pakistan Industrial Credit And Investment Corporation Limited (PICIC), presently Defendant-Respondent No.7, by way of creating a mortgage by depositing title deeds to establish a jute mill having 50 Nos. broadlooms; in addition to the foreign currency loan already obtained from PICIC, further Rupees 60,00,000.00 (six million) was required for the project and it was resolved that the money would be collected by issuing shares, having face value of Rs.10.00 each; it was further resolved that out of the requirements the sponsors of the company would manage/collect Rs. 30,00,000.00 (three million) and the rest Rs.30,00,000.00 (three million) would be collected from the different financial institutions and accordingly an agreement / contract was entered into, on 27/03/1070, under the name and style "UNDER WRITING-CUM-ADVANCE. 3. AGREEMENT", hereinafter referred to the 'AGREEMENT', between the defendant No.1-Apellant and eight (8) Nos. financial institutions including Pakistan Industrial Credit And Investment Corporation Limited '131C1C' and two predecessors of the plaintiff corporation; the financial institutions, as it reveals from the 'Agreement', are chronologically Nos. ii. Investment Corporation of Pakistan hereinafter referred to ICP iii. Pakistan Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation Limited (PICIC)', iv. Eastern Banking Corporation Limited hereinafter referred to EBCL, v. Premier Bank Limited hereinafter referred to PBL, vi. Habib Enterprises Limited hereinafter referred to KIEL, as being underwriter FIRST SET; Nos. vii. Eastern Federal Union Insurance Company Limited hereinafter referred to EFU, viii. Muslim Insurance Company Limited hereinafter referred to MICL, ix. Eastern Mercantile Insurance Company Limited hereinafter referred to EMIC, being underwriters SECOND SET. Under the said Agreement dated 27.03.70, predecessors of the plaintiff, namely 'EFU and MICL', hereinabove underwriter Nos. vii and viii `EFU and MICL' granted Rs.5,00,000.00 (five hundred thousand) only and Rs.2,50,000.00(Two hundred fifty thousand) only respectively as bridge loan to the defendant No. 1 Appellant on condition to issue 50,000 and 25,000 shares of Rs.10.00 each by the borrower/debtor-defendant No. 1; defendant Nos.2 and 3 are the signatories of the Agreement, Demand Promissory Note and letter of Indemnity etc; after the independence of Bangladesh the properties and obligations of the underwriters, namely `EFU and MICL' were vested with the government of Bangladesh and that in pursuance of President Order (PO) No. 95 of 1972 and Insurance Corporation Act, 1973 the bridge loan or advances of TRY and `MICL' amounting to Rs. 5,00,000.00 and Rs.2,50,000.00, total being Rs.7,50,000.00 along with interests were vested in the plaintiff; as stipulated in the Agreement dated 27.03,1970, the borrower defendants are bound and obligated to pay interests and penal interests on borrowed sum of Rs. 7,50,000.00; the defendant No. 1 did not repay the loan including interests even after repeated notices. Hence the suit. 

 4. Defendant Nos.1, 7 and 9 filed written statements; the case of defendant No.7, in short, is that the properties and obligations of underwriter No. iii. PICIC and ii. ICP were vested with the defendant No.7 and that PICIC granted the foreign currency loan to the defendant No. 1 to the tune of US $ 1.153 million equivalent to Rs. 5.534 million and to secure the loan the defendant No.1 deposited all its title deeds regarding all its immovable properties with the PICIC only; besides the foreign currency loan was guaranteed by the sponsors (defendant Nos. 2 and 3) of the company personally; the original title deeds of the immovable properties of the defendant No. 1 company are lying with the head office of PICIC at Karachi, Pakistan; the copy of the Agreement dated 27.03.1970 is not available with the defendant-Shangstha and the plaintiff is therefore put to prove their respective case and that this defendant does not have any comment regarding the transactions between plaintiff and defendant No.1 and that as at 01.01.1990 the defendant No. 1 company owes Tk. 1,1800,000.00 to defendant No.7 and that defendant No. 7 is not a necessary/proper party in the suit. Accordingly the contesting defendant No. 7 prayed for dismissal the suit with cost. 

 e. Is the plaintiff entitled to the decree as prayed for? 

 10. Mr. Saifur Reza, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant No.1 appellant took us through the pleadings of the suit and written statement, evidences, exhibits, and judgment and decree with relevant laws regarding to limitation of the suit. The appellant has nothing to submits regarding to issue Nos. 'a' to 'c' and `e' of the impugned judgment but admitted the facts and so far issue No. "d", of the said judgment is concerned the learned Advocate has submitted that the Court below committed multifaceted error of law and, as such, misdirected himself to arrive at a correct decision. He has further submitted that the learned Joint District Judge erroneously, both on facts and law, held that the suit is for sale of mortgaged property'; the learned Judge has also erroneously held that the suit is one under Artice-147 of the Limitation Act; the learned Judge has decided the issue in favour of the plaintiff relying on the fact that the defendant No. 1 in paragraph No. 20 of the written statement admitted that it had repaid Tk.1,00,000.00 only to the plaintiff on 12.01.1989, Therefore, the learned Judge opined that the loan was renewed and since, the learned Judge added, the suit is one under Article-147 of the Limitation Act the suit could have been filed within sixty(60) years and, the learned Joint District Judge further added, since sixty years’ time is yet to expire form 27.03.1970 the suit is not barred by limitation. He has next submitted that the finding regarding repayment by the defendant No.1 is, on the face of it, incorrect inasmuch as ext.6, 6(1) and (II) envisages that the defendant made repayment on 13.07.1970, 14.01.71 and 30.12.70 respectively. He has further added that admittedly the defendant made the last repayment on 14.01.1971 to the plaintiff after disbursement of the bridge loan by the predecessors of the plaintiff. He has next added that it is also admitted that the repayment dated 12.01.1989 was made after the suit was filed, on 29.10.1988, and it is also admitted that the said repayment was made after, at least, eighteen years after repayment dated 14.01.1971 (Ext. 6(1) of the disbursement of the loan money. He has next added that so far the finding of the learned Joint District Judge, regarding renewal or computation of fresh period of limitation of the loan money, is concerned, as reasoned by the learned Judge to arrive at as such is a wholesale error of law in view of section-20, read with Article-132 (C) and Artice-147 of the Limitation Act. He has next submitted that a plain reading makes it crystal clear that payment should be made on account of a debt before expiration of the prescribed period, but as the case in hand is concerned, payment was made firstly, after the suit was instituted and secondly, after eighteen years from due and thirdly, in view of Article-132 (c) of the Limitation Act, after the prescribed period of 12 (twelve) years; Article-132 ( C ) is the specified article for a suit for money only relating to mortgage by deposit of title deed. He has next added that the learned Judge erroneously found the Agreement dated 27.03.1970 (Ext.02) to be the 'mortgage by deposit of title deed' of which the plaintiff, as found by the learned Judge, to be the mortgaged; the definition of a mortgage by deposit of title deed has been contemplated in Section-58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, hereinafter referred to as 'T.P. Act'. He has next added that a plain reading of the unregistered Agreement / contract, namely' Underwriter-Cum-Advance' Agreement, reveals that the predecessors of the plaintiff were not mortgagees, rather predecessor of defendant No. 7(PICIC) was the mortgagee for the foreign currency loan from earlier without any memorandum of deposit of title deed; while the plaintiffs predecessors were parties to the said Agreement/Contract as financial institutions who did agree to sanction bridge loan to the defendant of which PICIC, being earlier mortgagee, stood security of the future bridge loan. He has further added that the Agreement is not a memorandum of deposit of title deed rather an unregistered Agreement/Contract and therefore inadmissible in evidence. He has next added that should the Agreement, for arguments sake, is considered to be an admissible 'memorandum of deposit of title deed' the expiration of limitation of such mortgage ought to have been read with Article 132 (c) of Limitation Act which provides 12 (twelve) years from the time when the money, sued for, becomes due, as the suit was filed more than 18(eighteen) years after money, sued for, became due the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation. He has further submitted that learned Judge erroneously held that the suit is one under Article-147 of the Limitation Act inasmuch as the said Article is applicable only in case of those mortgagees who are qualified to sell the mortgaged property in view of section 67 of the ' T. P. Act'. He has next submitted that a plain reading of Article-132( c ) with Article-147 of the Limitation Act and Section-67 (a) of the 'TT. Act' would make it crystal clear; that Section -67 of the T.P. Act' deals with the rights of the mortgagee to foreclose or sale subject to conditions as contemplated in clause Nos. (a) to (d). 

 11. Clause (a) of section 67 of the `T.P. Act' contemplates in the following manner: "S.67 Nothing in this section shall be deemed-"(a) to authorize any mortgagee other than a mortgagee by conditional sale or a mortgagee under an anomalous mortgage by the terms of which he is entitled to foreclose, to institute a suit for foreclosure, or an usufructuary mortgagee as such or a mortgagee by conditional sale as such to institute a suit for sale." 

 12. It has further submitted that the Agreement does not stipulate any term, whatsoever, empowering the alleged mortgagee to sale the alleged mortgaged property.
