parties:
Noor Alam ----- Defendant No. 3-Appellant
Vs
Sonali Bank & others ----- Plaintiff-Respondent
full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J: This appeal at the instance of appellant Noor Alam is directed against the Judgment and decree dated 23-11-1999 (decree signed on 4-1-2000) passed by the Sub-ordinate Judge, Additional Commercial Court No.1, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 145 of 1999 decreeing the suit. 

 2. Relevant facts of the case, in short, are that the respondent No.1, Sonali Bank as plaintiff filed a suit being Title Suit No.145 of 1999 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka impleading the present appellant Noor Alam and 2(two) others as defendants for realization of its outstanding dues amounting to Taka 4,43,888.50 with interest. The plaintiff's case in short, is that, the defendant No. 2 approached to the plaintiff-Bank vide his application dated 9-9-80 for issuance of a Bank Guarantee for Taka 6,50,000 for a period of one year to transact the normal business of defendant No.1 with Bangladesh Biman offering 15 Kathas of land as counter guarantee which valued at Taka 15,00,000 under Mouza Gulshan adjacent to Road No. 8 in Gulshan Model Town owned by the defendant No. 2, the proprietor of defendant No.1; that defendant No.3 vide his letter dated 15,9,1980 also prayed to the plaintiff-Bank to issue a Bank Guarantee for Taka 6,50,000 on behalf of the defendant No.1 of which defendant No. 2 is the proprietor offering his immovable property measuring 7½ Kathas of land with three-storied residential building situated thereon under Khatian No. 135 (New) and CS Khatian No. 14774 and C.S plot No. 28 in sheet No. 49 as described in the schedule 'B' of the plaint as security of the said Bank Guarantee; that the plaintiff-Bank through its Eskaton Road. Branch vide letter No. Eska/ BG-80/4 /1423 dated 1-10-1980 issued Bank Guarantee for Taka 6,50,000 for a period up-to 30th September, 1981 as required by them and thereupon, the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 mortgaged their property in favour of the plaintiff-bank as described in the schedule of the plaint; that on 22-11-1981 Bangladesh Biman, the beneficiary of the aforesaid Bank Guarantee, requested its Banker at Ramna Branch of the plaintiff-Bank to collect the amount of Taka 4,91,980/99 against the aforesaid Bank Guarantee for Taka 6,50,00.0 from the Eskaton Road Branch of the plaintiff-Bank and thereupon, the plaintiff-Bank on various occasions asked the defendant No. 2, to do the needful regarding the claim of the beneficiary Bangladesh Biman. The defendant No.2 instead of regularizing the Account filed a suit being TS No. 37 of 1981 in the Court of 3rd Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka for Temporary injunction restraining the plaintiff-Bank and the beneficiary-Bangladesh Biman, from encashing the Bank Guarantee dated 28-2-81 and obtained an order of status-quo with regard to encashment of the Bank Guarantee; that ultimately the aforesaid order of status-quo was vacated by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge Court, Dhaka vide order dated 29-7-81 and thereupon, unsuccessful-plaintiff filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 329 of 1981 in the Court of the leaned District Judge, Dhaka; that during the pendency of the aforesaid Misc. Appeal No. 329 of 1981 in the , Court of District Judge, Dhaka MLO No 14 was promulgated on 22nd April, 1982 and consequent thereupon by an order of the learned District Judge, Dhaka dated 28-6-1982 the aforesaid Misc. Appeal was struck off; that the defendant No. 1 was required to make marginal deposit of Taka 3,25,000 out of which Taka 2,61,000 was given by a cheque of Agrani Bank, Ramna branch against current account of the wife of the defendant No. 2 which was dishonored twice by the Bank. In spite of repeated reminder letters issued by the plaintiff bank to the defendant No. 2 for payment against the Bank Guarantee, nothing was done. Under this facts and circumstances the plaintiff-Bank was compelled to pay Taka 4,91,980.99 to the beneficiary, Bangladesh Biman on 17-10-82 under obligation for the Bank Guarantee on behalf of the defendant No. 1. Hence the suit. 

 3. The defendant No. 3 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaintiff contending, inter-alia, that the defendant No. 3 did not go to the plaintiff-Bank at any point of time, neither he mortgaged his property nor he became guarantor for anybody whatsoever; that some of the officers of the plaintiff-Bank in-collusion with defendant Nos. 1 and 2 prepared some forged documents in his name by way of false personating; that the defendant No.3 is not acquainted with the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in any manner and, as such, the question of being a guarantor for them by using his original title deed of 'B' schedule property does not arise at all; that due to missing of his original deed of his property relating to 'B' schedule of the plaint he lodged to GD dated 23-1-1978 and 14-10-1978 respectively and knowing about the suit as well as whereabouts of his original deed the defendant No.3 requested to the plaintiff-Bank to return his deed relating to "B-schedule" property of the plaint and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 5. The learned Subordinate Judge and Additional Artha Rin Adalat No. 1 heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and ultimately, on consideration of the evidences and other materials on record arrived at a finding that the plaintiff-Bank is entitled to get a decree as prayed for and accordingly, decreed the suit against the defendant No. 3 on contest and ex-parte against the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by his judgment and decree dated 23-11-1999 (decree signed on 4-1-2000). 

 21. At the trial the defendant No. 3 himself was examined as DW-1, Md Nur Alam, who in his deposition categorically stated that the defendant No. 2 in-collusion with some of the officers of the Bank on practicing fraud by using his missing deed created a forged counter bank-guarantee in his name. This witness in his deposition also stated that he had no relation with the defendant No. 1, that is, company of defendant No. 2 and the defendant No. 2 so the question to stand as guarantor for defendant Nos-1-2 by mortgaging his property does not arise at. all whatsoever. This witness also stated in his deposition that his original deed relating to "B-schedule" property was missing long before filling the instant suit and to that effect he lodged two GD with Sutrapur police station on 23-1-1978 and 14-10-1978 respectively, that is, long 3/4 years prior to filing the present suit on 29-2-1983. This witness also stated in his deposition that: একজিবিট-৪ যে জ্বাল সেটা প্রমান করার জন্য এক্সপার্ট অপিনিয়নের জন্য পাঠাতে চাই। This witness in his cross-examination denied the suggestion that on 29-9-1980 he went to the Sub-registrar office and executed power of attorney.

parties:
Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan and others ------ Petitioners
Vs
Kulsum Banu Bibi and others ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-2 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 31-1-2006 and 7-2-2006 respectively passed by the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria, in Title Appeal No. 7 of 2005 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 16-10-2004 and 21-10-2004 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kashba, Brahmanbaria, in Title Suit No. 28 of 2004 dismissing the suit should not be set aside. 

 2. The opposite party Nos.1, Kulsum Banu Bibi, 2. Tara Banu Bibi and 3. Md Abdur Rahim as plaintiffs instituted the Title Suit No. 52 of 1991 in the Court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kashba, Brahmanbaria impleading the above petitioner and others as defendants praying for a declaration that the compromise decree dated 8-11-90 passed in Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 is not binding upon them and the suit was subsequently transfer-red and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 53 of 1998 and lastly it was transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Kashba, Brahmanbaria and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 28 of 2004 for trial. 

 3. That the case of the plaintiffs-opposite parties in brief are that Pandit Chandra Rudra Paul and Swarup Chandra Paul were original owners of the suit land of schedule No. 1 and while they were possessing and enjoying the property Kushai Chandra Das and Aswini Kumar Das purchased the same from them and became the owner and possessor of the land. Aswini Kumar Das died leaving behind 4 sons Ambika Charan Das, Paresh Das, Animesh Das and Amalesh Das and Kushai Chandra Das died leaving behind 2 sons Anil Chandra Das and Monindra Chandra Das and accordingly, RS Khatian No. 43 was prepared in their name. Ambika Charan Das and others while they were possessing and enjoying the property in the year 1963 they exchanged the said land with the land of one Moulavi Abdul Matin of Kasharmara Mouza of Police Station Radhakishorepur of Tripura, India and in this way Abdul Ma tin became owner and possessor of the schedule land. Moulvi Abdul Ma tin while owning and possessing the land on 28-12-64 exchanged .39 acres of land with plaintiff No. 1 and her husband Badsha Mia became owner and possessor of the same. In this way the plaintiff became owner of 0.39½ acres i.e. 0.39½ acres by exchange and 0.15 acres by purchase and thereafter sold 0.20 acres to plaintiff No. 2 who remained owner and possessor of rest 0.14½ acres of land. 

 4. Badsha Mia while owning and possessing 0.19½ acres of land along with others permitted defendant No. 2 to reside there temporarily as he became 'Peer' of Badsha and Badsha was his Murid as religious guide. Tara Banu opposite party No. 2 got her 0.04 acres of land as heirs. Subsequently Chan Mia and Jarina Begum and other heirs of Badsha Mia sold 0.12 acres of land to Tara Banu and in her way Tara Banu became the owner and possessor of 0.16 acres of land and when Nawab Mia husband of Tara Banu went to the Tahshil office for separation of Jama after paying rent on 10-1-91 then came to know that the defendant No. 2 vide Mutations Case No. 354/85-86 mutated his name in respect of 0.54 acres of land in Plot Nos. 166, 167 and 168. Thereafter the plaintiff on 21-1-1991 went to the office of Assistant Commissioner, Akhaura and came to know that a review case was pending against the said mutation case, then the plaintiff filed an application thereon for addition of party and Assistant Commissioner directed the parties to appear before him with necessary papers but the defendant No. 2 failed to show any papers in support of their title, that on 13-2-1991 the defendant No. 2 expressed that his brother-in-law, the defendant No. 1, was the owner of the land on the basis of the title suit and prayed for affirming the order of mutation, on 16-2-1991. The husband of plaintiff No. 1 searched for the suit and on 12-3-1991 after getting certified copy of the same came to know about the collusive compromise judgment and decree of the Title Suit No. 78 of 1988. The plaintiffs of the suit are the owners and possessors of the suit land knowing fully well that the plaintiffs of the instant suit land filed the Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 without making the plaintiffs as parties of the said suit and, as such, prayed for a decree that the compromise decree dated 8-11-1990 passed in Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 was collusive and not binding upon him. 

 5. The defendant Nos. 1-2(Ka)-2(Ja) contested the said suit by filing two separate sets of written statement denying all the material allegation of the plaint. The case of the defendant No. 1, in short, is that the original owner of the land was Ambika Charan Das and others and they sold the property to defendant No. 1 as at that time there was some restrictions in registration of minority properties, as such, a bainapatra was executed and the defendant No. 1 paid the rent to the Government and the brother-in-law (sister's husband) of defendant No. 1 used to possess and enjoy the suit land by erecting houses and establishing a Madrasha therein. That Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 was decreed on compromise with defendant No. 2 was rightly and properly passed and, as such, the instant suit should be dismissed. 

 6. The defendant Nos. 2(Ka)-2(Ja) also contested the suit by filing separate written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaint stating, inter alia, that the defendant No. 2 Moulvi Deen Mohammad was a great Alem, he was the Khalifa of Sonakanda Darbar who had many disciples, the plaintiffs' predecessor Badsha Mia was also a Murid of defendant No. 2 and sold the land to defendant No. 2 by a registered deed No. 6699 dated 25-11-68 and on the same date executed a registered compensation deed No. 6700. Consequently, the defendant No. 2 during his lifetime had been living in the suit land by erecting houses and lived therein with his family and also established a Madrasha set up tube-well, latrine, etc. When the defendant No. 1 claimed the suit land and filed the Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 against the original owners, the defendant No. 2 filed a solehnama to get a compromise decree then the aforesaid compromise decree was passed. The plaintiff's predecessors Badsha Mia had no right title and possession in the suit land and in the recent survey operation when surveyor found defendant No. 2 in the suit land he prepared RS Khatian in his name correctly and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 4. Whether the plaintiffs are entitled to get a decree as prayed for and 

 5. Whether the plaintiffs are entitled to get any other relief. 

 11. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, the plaintiff No. 1. Kulsum Banu, the wife of Badsha Mia and plaintiff No. 2 Tara Banu, the daughter of Badsha Mia filed an appeal before the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria being Title Appeal No. 7 of 2005, the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria himself heard the title appeal and allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court by his judgment and decree dated 31-1-2006 and 3-2-2006 respectively. 

 13. The learned Counsel Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali with Mr Biswajit Chakraborty, appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-petitioner, submits that the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria was absolutely wrong and erroneous in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. The learned trial Court, after examining the evidence on record and discussing all the issues framed by him whether the suit is maintainable in its present form or not and other issues, passed the judgment and decree dismissing the suit of the plaintiff which was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Next he submits that the learned trial Court committed no error in. deciding the issues and rightly held that the plaintiff miserably failed to prove the case, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court was absolutely right and justified which should not be assailed by the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali next submits that the lower appellate Court while reversing the finding of the trial Court he should assign a cogent and reasonable ground and the finding of the trial Court should be reversed with reference to the evidence on record, but the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria committed a gross illegality in not referring the finding of the trial Court, particularly with regard to the law point which is liable to be set aside and interfered by this Court. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali further submits that the finding of the trial Court, particularly on 2 points, that the suit is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the plaintiff No. 2 during the pendency of the trial of the suit by submitting a compromise petition and relinquished his claim over 20 decimals of the suit land in Plot Nos. 166-167 and accordingly, the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 ought to have corrected the schedule of the suit land. But the lower appellate Court did not mention a single word in his judgment on these two points i.e. with regard to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the compromise petition filed by the plaintiff No. 2 who has relinquished his claim and also did not file any appeal. This sort of non-consideration in finding of the lower appellate Court in reversing the judgment of the trial Court appears to be manifestly perverse which is liable to be interfered by this Court. The learned Counsel finally submits that admittedly the defendants had been in possession of the suit land since long so in a suit for declaration without seeking a consequential relief for recovery of khas possession is not at all maintainable. The PWs 2 and 3 in cross-examination categorically stated in their evidence that Deen Mohammed, the defendant No. 2, had been living in the suit land with his family members by erecting houses. PW 3 further stated in his evidence that defendant No. 2 Deen Mohammad was a good man and he was in possession of the suit land. He also submits that the lower appellate Court did not at all discuss the evidence of PWs and DWs. Md Ruhul Amin, son of Deen Mohammad was examined as DW 1 and after the death of Deen Mohammad during the pendency of the suit who was living in the suit land categorically stated in his evidence about the title and possession of the suit land and exhibited the registered title deed in original dated 25-11-68 which was exhibited as Exhibit-Ka. The registered deed Exhibit-Ka, the original purchase deed of the defendant obviously shows that the vendor of that deed Kulsum and Tara Banu along with others were the vendor who are now plaintiff Nos. 1-3 respectively and in that deed the vendee was Deen Mohammad the defendant No. 2 and since the purchase of the suit land in the year 1968 after the death of Badsha Mia the defendant has been living in the suit land with his other family members. 

 The learned lower appellate Court did not at all consider the evidence of DW with regard to the title deed and also the proof of possession of the defendant which was admitted by PWs 2 and 3, as such, the defendant successfully proved the title and possession in the suit land. Therefore, the learned trial Court properly dismissed the suit which was absolutely correct and justified. The finding of the appellate Court in reversing the finding of the trial Court transpires to be manifestly perverse which is liable to be interfered by this Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and hence the Rule should be made absolute. The learned Counsel, before conclusion of his argument in support of his contention made above, referred the case of Nurul Islam (Babul) vs Shanti Rani Dhupi and others reported in 12 MLR (AD) 105 wherein it has been stated: 

 Section 42. When the plaintiff is not in possession of suit land no decree for declaration of title can be granted without seeking for recovery of possession". 

 14. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr Zulfiqur Ahmed, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party, submits that the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria was absolutely right and justified in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court which is not liable to be disturbed in revision by the High Court Division. Next he submits that the appellate Court, after discus-sing the evidence on record and perusing the exhibits, papers and documents produced by both the parties and after proper assessment of the evidence on record, came to his finding that the plaintiff could be able to prove the case successfully, as such, the suit was decreed in favour of the plaintiff. He further submits that the finding of facts, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court is final which is not liable to be disturbed by this Court. He also submits that the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria elaborately discussed the evidence on record and also found that the defendant on the basis of a forged solehnama decree tried to establish his claim over the suit land which is not legally tenable. He further submits that the defendant attained the fraudulent compromised decree in Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 which cannot be the basis of his title. The learned trial Court dismissed the suit of the plaintiff merely on technical ground that the plaint was not properly prepared. Finally, he submits that since there is no non-reading, misreading and non-consideration of material evidence on record the finding of the lower appellate Court is not liable to be disturbed by the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 15. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, exhibits, registered deed, documents and also the judgment of both the Courts below it appears that the trial Court discussed the evidence and also perused the documents and legal aspect of the case and made his observation that the suit was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned trial Court further held in his judgment that since PWs 2 and 3 admitted the possession of the defendant in the suit land the plaintiff ought to have sought for recovery of khas possession as consequential relief. But the plaintiff instituted a simple suit for declaration of title which is not maintainable and hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria while reversing the judgment of the trial Court did not write a single word about this specific finding of the law point by the trial Court which appears to be manifestly perverse. Moreover, when the plaintiff No. 2 during the pendency of the suit in the trial Court by submitting a compromise petition relinquished his claim over 20 decimals of the suit land then the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 3 ought to have amended the schedule of the suit land but the plaintiffs did not do so. This observation made by the trial Court was absolutely correct but the lower appellate Court did not at all consider this vital and material point and did not mention anything in his judgment on this point. The lower appellate Court while reversing the judgment of the trial Court is required to reverse the material finding of the trial Court with reference to the evidence on record but the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria did not do so. The lower appellate Court should assign cogent and reasonable ground in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court. In this connection I like to rely on the decision in the case of Ranajit Sarker vs Sree Sukhendu Bikash Biswas reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 58 = 2 BLC (AD) 100 wherein it has been held: 

 18. The discussion made above and the facts and legal position of the case, the impugned judgment and decree dated 31-1-2006 and 7-2-2006 respectively passed by the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria, in Title Appeal No. 7 of 2005 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 16-10-2004 and 21-10-2004 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kashba, Brahmanbaria, in Title Suit No. 28 of 2004 dismissing the suit is hereby set aside and the impugned judgment and decree passed by the trial Court is hereby affirmed.

parties:
Humayun Hossain Khan  ------- Petitioner 
Vs. 
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
The petitioner obtained a loan of Taka 7,50,000 on 12-9-1989 from Sonali Bank (hereinafter called 'the Bank') in order to complete the unfinished construction of his house on Plot No. 45, Road No.7, Sector-4 of Uttara Model Town, Dhaka (hereinafter referred to as 'the house'). Accordingly, he mort- gaged the house in terms of a mortgage deed registered on 6-5-1990 in favour of the Bank. The petitioner also executed some other documents for securing the loan. The petitioner obtained the loan with simple interest of Taka 13.6% per annum. But the petitioner could not let out the house at an expected rent as a result of which he failed to pay the regular instalments to the Bank and requested the Bank for re-scheduling the outstanding debt with simple interest. But the Bank instituted Title Suit No. 15 of 2003 before the Court of Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. I, Dhaka against the petitioner on January 27, 2003 for realisation of the loan along with the interest amounting to Taka 38,06,058 as on 31-12-2002 and also for other reliefs. The petitioner as defendant No. I contested the suit by filing a written statement. The said suit was subsequently transferred to the Artha Rin Adalat No.3, Dhaka (hereinafter referred to as the Adalat) and renumbered as Artha Rin Suit No. 32 of 2004. After the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (hereinafter called as the Ain, 2003) came into force on 1st May, 2003, settlement conference was also held under section 21 of the Ain, 2003 on prayer of the Bank. Defendant No. 1 (petitioner) filed in the Adalat an application on 20-8-2004 under Order XIV, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (shortly, the Code) with a prayer to fix the total money payable to the Bank at Taka 11,50,000 by applying the provisions of section 47 read with section 60 of the Ain, 2003. But the Adalat rejected the said application by the impugned order. Hence, this writ petition. 

 (1) The original Title Suit No. 15 of2003 was filed before the Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka against the defendant-petitioner on 27-1-2003 when the Ain 2003 did not come into play. So, the provisions of section 47 of the Ain, 2003 was not applicable to the suit and thus, the impugned order dated 4-10-2004 passed by the Adalat was in accordance with law.
