parties:
Surendra Nath Halder & ors ------Appellant
Vs.
Satyandra Nath Halder ------Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Daliluddin Ahmed, J:—This Rule is directed against judgment and decree, dated 6.11.81 passed by the Additional District Judge, Its Court, Bakerganj in Title Appeal No. 42 of 1978, reversing those, dated 30.12.77, passed by the Munsif, 2nd Court, Perojpur in Title Suit No. 199 of 1983. 

 2. The plaintiffs petitioners instituted Title Suit No, 199 of 1983 in the Court of Munsif, Perojour against the defendants-opposite parties for declaration of their title to the suit land and for confirmation of possession therein. The plaintiffs case, inter-alia. was that the suit land measuring 70 acres belonged to the defendant Nos. 4, 5 and one Laxmi Kanta, the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1-3. The said owners orally leased out the suit land to the defendant Nos. 7-11 on the 15th Baisakh, 1360 B.S at an annual rental of Rs. 5 annas 12 only on receipt of proper salami and delivered possession of the leased out land to the lessees. Thereafter the lessees executed a registered kabuliyat, dated 25.1.55 in favour of their lessors. These lessees had been in possession of the suit land and while so possessing they sold the land to the plaintiffs, by a registered kabala, dated 31.3.58 and delivered possession to them. Since their purchase, the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land. The land has been wrongly recorded in the name of the previous owners. The defendant No. 6 fraudulently auction purchased the land on 7.11.62 in certificate sale in pursuance of the Certificate Case No. 1836 of 1959 against the original owners who had no subsisting interest. Defendant No. 6 did not acquire any title or interest in the suit property and he also did not get possession of the same. In Baishakh 1370 B.S. the defendants No. 6 threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs from suit land which clouded the title of the plaintiffs. Hence the suit has been filed. 

 3. The defendant No. 6 (the present opposite party No. 1) contested the suit by filing a written statement. He admitted that the suit land originally belonged to the defendant Nos. 4, 5 and Laxmi Kanta, the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1-3, but be has denied all other allegations made in the plaint. He contended that the alleged oral lease of the suit land by the original owners to the defendant Nos. 7-11 on the  15th Baishak, 1360 B.S. is fraudulent, collusive, in-operative and void. The defendant Nos. 7-11 did not possess the property on the basis of the lease. He also denied the validity of the registered kabala, dated 31.3.58 and contended that the plaintiffs acquired no right, title and possession of the suit land on the basis of the said kabala. His further case was that the suit land was put to auction sale in certificate case No. 1830 of 1959 started against the original owners and he (the defendant No. 6) auction purchased the same on 7-11-62 and got delivery of possession on 23.11.62. Since then the defendant No. 6 has been possessing the suit land. The plaintiffs have neither title nor possession and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 4. The predecessor of the present learned Munif decreed the suit against the defendant No. 6 and ex-parte against the rest. Being aggrieved by the decision, the defendant preferred Title Appeal N. 167 of 1975 and the appellate court sent back the suit on remand to the court of Munsif for holding a fresh trial with certain observations. Thereafter learned Munsif after fresh hearing decreed the suit by his judgment and decree, dated 30.12.77. Again being aggrieved by the decision of the learned Munsif, the defendant No. 6 preferred title appeal No. 42 of 1978, which was allowed by the learned Additional District Judge, Its Court, Bakerganj by his judgment and decree dated 6.11.81 setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif. 

 Admittedly the suit land originally belonged to the defendant Nos. 4 and 5 and Laxmi Kanta, the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1-3. The plaintiff claim that the original owners orally leased out the suit land to defendant Nos. 7-11 on the 5th Baisakh, 1360 B.S. and subsequently the lessees executed a registered kabuliyat, Ext. 2, on 25.11.55 in favour of the lessors. It is also the plaintiff's case that the lessees (i.e. defendant Nos. 7-11) possessed the suit land and sole the same to the plaintiffs by kabala, dated 31.3.58. Ext. 1. The contestant defendant opposite party No. 1 denied the oral lease and maintained that the registered kabuliyat, Ext. 2, was fraudulent and void. 

 6. The appellate court on consideration of evidence on record and the legal aspect of the case has found that the kabuliyat, dated 25.1.66, Ext. 2, is hit by section 15-A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (herein after called the Act) and the said lease was null and void and as such the land stood forfeited to Government. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioners, has frankly admitted that the basic document of the plaintiffs' title, i.e. Ext. 2, is hit by the provisions of section 75-A. of the Act and on the basis of the said kabuliyat, Ext. 2 and the kabala, Ext. 1, the plaintiffs have not acquired any title to the suit land. But he contended that as the kabuliyat, Ext. 2, is null and void, the title to the suit land will remain unaffected with the lessors and the land can not be legally forfeited Mr. Hemayet Uddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 6 (opposite party No. 1) has argued that provisions of sub-section (2) of section 75-A of the Act indicate that forfeiture will operate at once and the Government will acquit light to the land as soon as sub-letting is made in contravention of sub-section (1) of the said section. Now the question that arises from the facts and circumstances of the case is; that to whom the suit land will go on the violation of sub-section (1) of section 75-A of the Act. i.e. whether title to the suit land would remain with leaser or it would vest with the Government. 

 9. Sub-section (1) of section 75-A of the Act provides that on and from the date of notification referred to above, no person shall sub-let any land in his khas possession and sub-section (2) provides that any sub-letting in contravention of sub-section (1) shall strand null, and void. There was no penal provision in section 75-A of the Act at the time of granting of the impugned lease by kabuliyat, dated 25.1.55, Ext. 2. The portion and the land so sub-let shall stand forfeited to the provincial Government in sub-section (2) of section 75-A was added by section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition (Amendment), 1956 (East Bengal Act 1V of 1956) and came into force on 13.4.56. There is nothing in the. East Bengal Act IV of 1956 to indicate that the penal provision was given retrospective effect. The penal laws should be strictly construed and retrospective effect should not be given to such provisions unless such intention clearly appears from the Statute itself. So, I am constrained to hold on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant laws that the impugned lease by kabuliyat, dated 25.1.55, Ext. 2, was hit by sub-section (2) being in contravention of sub-section (1) of section 75-A of the Act and the lease was null and void; but the lease being void ab initio the title to the suit land remained with the lessers (i.e. defendant Nos. 4, 5 and Laxmi Kanta, the predecessor of defendant Nos. 1-3) and the plaintiffs did not acquire any title to the suit land by kabala, dated 31.3.58, Ext. 1. I also hold that the learned Appellate Court was wrong is holding that the suit land stood forfeited to the Government. The decision reported in 21 DLR page 511 (Mokbul Ahmed, Contractor vs. Md. Idris and others) relied upon by the appellate court is distinguishable. In the reported decision, the impugned lease was granted on 28.8.56 and 24 9.56 i.e. after the penal provision was added to sub-section (2) of section 75-A. But in the present case the impugned lease was granted on 25.1.55, i.e. prior to the date of passing of Act IV of 1956. Hence I hold that the decision reported in 21 DLR page 511 is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the present case. 

 10. From the perusal of record, it appears that the suit land was not forfeited to the Government rather it was treated as the property belonging to the lessor (i.e. original owners). The Government acquired the rent receiving interest in Perojpur Sub-Division including the disputed Daihari Mouza, J.L. 37, P.S. Swarupkati, with effect from 15th April, 1955, corresponding to 1st Baisakh, 1362 B.S. and the superior interest of the landlords was acquired and the defendant Nos. 4, 5 and Laxmi Kanta were treated as tenants under Government and was recorded as such in the S.A. khatian. Thereafter the suit land was put to auction sale by the Government in Certificate case No. 1380 of 1959 started against defendant Nos. 4, 5 and Laxmi Kanta and the suit land was auction purchased by the defendant No. 6 (opposite party No. 1) on 7.11.62 and he got symbolical possession against judgment-debtors (vide Ext. B.) 

 11. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-petitioners has contended that the appellate court having found that the plaintiffs have been in possession of the suit land adversely against the interest of the owners, they have acquired an indefeasible title to the suit and the appellate court erred in law in not decreeing the suit on declaration of the plaintiffs title to the suit land by adverse possession. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has relied upon the decision reported in 28 DLR page 256 (Abdus Sattar Sikder vs. Imam Hossain). 

 12 Both the courts below have found that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land since the date of their void kabala dated 31.3.58, Ext. 1. P.W, 4 Khirod Haldar, who is a very competent witness to depose regarding possession has supported the plaintiffs case regarding possession that he plaintiffs possess the land in the last 16/17 years. Agreeing with the court below, I also bed that the plaintiffs have been in uninterrupted possession of the suit land adversely against the right, title and interest of the original owners since 31.8.68. 

 13. It is true that the defendant No. 6 auction purchased the property and got symbolical possession through courts, but there is nothing on suit record to show that he got actual physical possession of the suit land. The defendant No. 6 examined D.Ws. 4. and 5 to prove his possession of the suit land, but they have been disbelieved by the courts below. The record shows that the plaintiffs were neither parties to the Certificate case not to the Execution proceedings. Symbolical possession obtained by the defendant No. 6 will not affect the plaintiffs possession as they were not parties to the execution proceeding. So, I bold that the plaintiffs' on the basis of an invalid kabala, Ext. 1, got possession in the suit land and have been in possession of the same asserting their own right adversely to the real owners for more than 12 years and as such they have acquired an indefensible title to the suit land. In this regard, I may refer to the decision reported in 16 DLR page 287 (Mir Laik Ali Khan vs. Standard Vacuum Oil co.) wherein it has been held by their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan as follows: 

 "As such the defendants no. 11 did not acquire any title in the property by virtue of the kabuliyat dated 25.1.55 Ext. 2 and consequently, the plaintiffs also acquired no title in the land by virtue of their kabala dated 31.3,58 Ext. 1". 

 15. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, I also find that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land since the date of their purchase by the invalid kabala dated 31.3 58, Ext. 1 and they have been in uninterrupted possession of the same asserting their own right against the rightful owners for more that 12 years and as such they have acquired an indefeasible title to the suit land by adverse possession. 

 16. Now the question is whether the plaintiffs are entitled to a decree for declaration of their title to the suit land on the basis of adverse possession. Mr. Hemayetuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 (defendant No. 61 has submitted that as the plaintiffs not having pleaded adverse possession in the plaint and no issue regarding adverse possession having been framed, the plaintiffs are not entitled to a decree. In the present case, the plaintiffs did not specifically take the plea of adverse possession but the question of possession is in the plaint and an issue in the suit, and both the parties were aware regarding the question of possession and adduced evidence in support of their respective plea of possession. The contesting defendant was neither prejudiced nor was taken by surprise. This being the position, there is no bar against passing a decree in favour of the plaintiffs on the basis of adverse possession. On consideration of similar facts and circumstances, Mr. Justice Abdur Rahman Chowdhury in 28 DLR page 256 (Abdul Saltar Vs. Imom Hossain and others) has held as follows:— 

 17. Both the courts below have elaborately considered the evidence on record and have arrived at the concurrent finding that the plaintiff has been in continuous possession since the date of his settlement which was well over 12 years and as such he has acquired good and valid title by adverse possession. 

 18. So, on consideration of evidence on record and the relevant laws, I find that the plaintiffs have been in uninterrupted actual physical possession of the suit land asserting their own rights and against the right, title and interest of the original owner since the date of their purchase which is well over 12 years and as such they have acquired valid title to the suit land by adverse possession and they are entitled to a decree in their favour.

parties:
Jamir Ali and others --------- Plaintiffs-Appellants
Vs.
Bangladesh, represented by Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, Collectorate Building, P. S. - Kotwali, District-Dhaka and another --------- Defendants-respondents
full_judgment:
Mohi Uddin Shamim, J: 1. This appeal, at the instance of the plaintiffs-appellants, is directed against the judgment and decree dated 26.07.2009 (decree signed on 02.08.2009) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 221 of 2005 dismissing the suit. 

 2. Facts relevant for disposal of the appeal are that one Paku Bepari originally owned 4.29 acres of land in C.S. Plot No. 1131 under Khatian No. 514 of Vanderkhola Mouza. He sold 52 decimals to Ashraf Ali, and 19.50 decimals each to Warish Ali and Mohammad Ali. After his death, his remaining 3.375 acres of land passed in ejmali to his five sons namely Wahed Ali, Chunnu Miah, Lal Miah, Nannu Miah, and Mojibor. Out of the said 375 acres of land, 1.43 acres were recorded in the name of Nannu Miah in S.A. Plot No. 1416 under S. A. Khatian No. 675, while 1.94 acres remained unrecorded. However, each of the sons of Paku Bepari effectively received 67.50 decimals land. Thereafter, Chunnu Miah and Lal Miah together orally gifted their 1.33 acres to Wahed Ali, in this way Wahed Ali became owner of 202.5 decimals of land, out of which 1.95 acres were recorded in his name in Plot No. 716 under S.A. Khatian No. 763. Wahed Ali died leaving behind a son Abbas Uddin and a daughter Edon Nessa as of his legal heir. Abbas Uddin and Edon Nessa together transferred 91 decimals of land by registered Deed No. 2874 on 26.06.1980 to the plaintiffs’ No. 1 - 4. They also transferred 1.04 acres of land to plaintiff No. 5 on the same date by registered Deed No. 2875. On 19.04.1999, Mohammad Ali transferred 19.50 decimals of land by registered Deed No. 2393 from S. A. Khatian No. 677 to Chunnu Miah. In this way Chunnu Miah became the owner of 87 (67.5+19.5) decimals of land. On 02.03.2002, Chunnu Miah transferred 65 decimals of land to plaintiff No. 1 by registered Deed No. 2225. On 14.05.2002, one of the sons of Paku Bepari namely Mojibur Rahman transferred 26 decimals to plaintiffs No. 1 - 4 by registered Deed No. 5439. As a result, plaintiff No. 1 became the owner of 94.25 decimals of land and plaintiffs No. 2, 3 and 4 each held 29.25 decimals of land and plaintiff No. 5 held 1.04 acres. On 29.09.2002, the plaintiffs being owner of 2.86 acres land mutated the property in their names. It is claimed that 100 acres land, including the suit land, were eroded by the river Dhalweshory before the R.S. survey, and hence the same were recorded in the name of the Government in Khatian No. 1 in RS Khatian, prepared and published in the year 1970. The land reappeared in 1974 and became arable, but the R.S. record remained unchanged, clouding plaintiffs’ title. Hence the suit seeking a declaration of title and that the R.S. record in the Government’s name is illegal, collusive, and fraudulent. 

 iii. whether the plaintiffs have right, title, interest and possession in the suit property? 

 7. Mr. Md. Faruque Ahammed, learned Advocate along with Mr. M. A. Mannan Bhuiyan appearing for the plaintiffs-appellants, at the very outset submits that the documentary evidence and witness testimonies clearly establish that the plaintiffs’ predecessors were the rightful owners of the suit land, and that the plaintiffs acquired valid title through lawful transfers. He contends that the trial Court committed serious errors of law and fact by failing to consider these material aspects of the suit and thereby reached an erroneous decision, occasioning a failure of justice. He further submits that, under the principle of reformation, the plaintiffs’ right, title, and interest in the suit land remain unaffected and the plaintiffs being in possession thereof till date, the trial Court erred in law holding that their right, title and interest over the suit land stood extinguished. He next submits that the R. S. record prepared in 1970 indicates that the suit land had already been reappeared in its original position prior to the enforcement of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (“hereinafter referred to as ‘Act, 1950’), and thus the plaintiffs’ case does not fall within the mischief of those provisions. And the trial Court, he argues, failed to properly interpret and apply the relevant provisions of the Act. He lastly submits that, Exhibits 1 - 10 establish the plaintiffs’ valid title and interest over the lands, while Exhibit “Ka” disproves the claim that the land reappeared only after section 86 came into force. The trial Court, by disregarding these crucial facts, again reached an incorrect and erroneous decisions, resulting in manifest injustice. In support of his submission, the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-appellants cited a decision in the case of Abi Abdullah (Md) and others Vs. Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land and others, reported in 58 DLR 250 wherein their lordship’s held to the effect that; “ …… The intention of amending section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1994 is public interest and for benefit of the tenants who owned and possessed land as of own right before diluvion and also after alluvion and, as such, retrospective operation of the Act may be attracted in appropriate cases. The petitioner’s case is a fit one to receive such interpretation. …. ” 

 9. In reply, Ms. Ainun Naher, learned Deputy Attorney General, with Mr. Md. Mozammel Hossain, learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the defendant-respondent No. 1, takes us through the impugned judgment, written statement, and other materials available on record, and submits that, it is admitted by the contesting parties that 4.29 acres of land in S.A. Khatian No. 1416 of Vandarkhola Mouza has been recorded in R.S. Plot No. 2786 in Khatian No. 1. She also submits that, the plaintiff No. 1, as P.W.1, admitted in his deposition stating as “ আমাদের এলাকায় ১৯৭০ ইং সনে R S রেকর্ড হয়। ১৯৬৭ ইং সনে না: জমি নদীগর্ভে বিলীন হয়। ১৯৭৪ সনে উহা নদী হতে ফেরত আসে।” She submits that the core legal issue needs to be addressed here is the application and interpretation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and its various amendments, particularly the Fourth Amendment by President Order, namely the Bangladesh State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972 (hereinafter, referred as ‘P O No. 135 of 1972’). Ms. Naher further contends that under the amended section 86 introduced by P.O. No. 135 of 1972 the right, title, and interest of a tenant in land lost by diluvion stands extinguished, whether the loss occurred before or after the amendment came into force. Since the land in question was lost by diluvion in 1967 and reappeared in 1974, thus the plaintiffs’ claim is barred by the clear language of the statute. In this context, the learned Deputy Attorney General has cited a decision in the case of the Government of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh and others Vs. Md. Kazemuddin Miah, reported in 21 BLC (AD) 186, wherein their lordship’s held that; 

 “The right, title and interest of the tenant or his successor-in-interest shall subsist during the period of loss if the land re-appear in situ within thirty years of loss is so clear and unambiguous that the legislature intended this provision to have prospective operation. The use of the word ‘shall’ is taken to indicate that the statue is to be construed as prospective only. The words ‘within thirty years of loss’ means if the diluvion takes place after 13th July, 1994, the tenant or his successor’s right to repossession shall subsist if the diluviated land re-appear within thirty years of loss and not otherwise. The amendment is prospective in operation.” 

 12. It appears from the record that the present appellants as plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration of title in the suit land and also for declaration that R.S. record of right of the suit land prepared in the name of the defendant-Government is illegal, collusive and fraudulent. The claim of the plaintiffs is that they are owners of the suit land by purchase and they mutated the same in their names on 29.09.2002. Their case is that 100 acres of land including the suit land were diluviated in the river Dhalwesshory and consequently, during the preparation of R.S. record of right the suit property was recorded in the name of the Government in 1970. It is stated in the plaint that, the suit property along with other properties re-appeared in 1974 and became arable for cultivation. 

 14. The trial Court on examination of the evidence of PWs came to a finding that the suit property was diluviated in the river Dholwesshory in 1967 and the same re-appeared in 1974. Accordingly, the trial Court held that since the land deluviated reappeared of the land took place after 1963 i.e. after coming into force of Part-V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950; the right, title and interest of the suit land has been vested to the Government and extinguishes those right, title and interest of the original owners as per section 86(3) of the said Act. On such findings the trial Court dismissed the suit. 

 15. Upon detailed examination of the testimonies, it appears that P.W.1, Jamir Ali, testified in support of the plaintiffs’ case, identifying himself as plaintiff No. 1 and a close relative of the other plaintiffs. He provided a detailed narration of the chain of title starting from the original owner Paku Bepari and described various transfers by inheritance and registered sale deeds, including Deeds No. 2873, 2874, 2393, 2225, and 5439, by which the plaintiffs allegedly acquired a total of 2.86 acres. He stated that mutation was completed in their names and referred to certified copies of mutation and relevant Khatians. He claimed that the suit land was lost to river erosion in 1967, reappeared in 1974, and that the plaintiffs took possession thereafter by identifying boundaries and cultivating the land. P.W.1 denied fabricating any documents or filing the suit to harass the government and grab the lands and asserted that their ownership and possession had continued uninterrupted after the land's reappearance. He also stated that R.S. recording in Khatian No. 1 in the name of the Government was erroneous, as at the time of R.S. survey, the land was submerged, and thus recorded as government khas land by default. 

 23. Let us appreciate the provision of section 86. Relevant provision is thus quoted below: “86 (2). Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successors-in-interest shall be extinguished in such lands or portion thereof, whether the loss of such lands or portion by diluvion took or takes place before or after the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972. (3) All lands, so lost by diluvion under sub-section(2), which re-appeared before the date of commencement of the said Order, but in respect of which the right of tenant, whose land was so lost, or his successors-in-interest, to repossession was not finally recognized or declared by a competent authority or Court under any law for the time being in force and also all lands, so lost by diluvion under the said sub-section, which may re-appear on or after the said date, shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and shall be at its disposal.” 

 25. Upon consideration of the oral testimonies of P.W.1 to P.W.3 and D.W.1, it appears that the plaintiffs have attempted to establish their claim through a chain of title (P.W.1) and corroborative testimony regarding the land’s diluvion in 1967 - 68 and reappearance in 1974 (P.W.2 and P.W.3). Since the plaintiff’s themselves admitted alluvion in 1974, the title to land, admittedly vests in the Government upon clear extinguishment of the rights of all other previous owners of land. The submission made by the learned Advocate for the Appellant to the effect that the land alluviated before 1970 is incorrect and not supported by evidence on record. The absence of corroboration from competent land authorities regarding the appellant’s alleged “continuous” possession also weakens the plaintiff’s claim. 

 30. The judgment and decree dated 26.07.2009 (decree signed on 02.08.2009) passed by the Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 221 of 2005 is hereby affirmed and maintained.

Md Nuruzzaman, J: This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order 19-4-2009 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1084 of 1998 discharging the Rule arising out of the judgment and decree dated 20-10-1997 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Lakshmipur, in Title Appeal No.107 of 1991 reversing the judgment and decree dated 30-9-1991 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Lakshimpur in Title Suit No.253 of 1983 decreeing the suit. 

 The plaintiffs-appellants instituted Title Suit No.253 of 1983 before the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Lakshmipur, praying for decree for declaration of title in the suit land measuring an area of 2.44 acres stating, inter alia, that the suit land of DS Khatian No.126 of Romapur Mouza belonged to Muzaffar Ahmed and others. In four annas share, Muzaffar Ahmed was the owner of 991/2 decimals of land and he sold 73 decimals of land to the plaintiff No.1 by a registered deed of sale dated 28-1-1959. Maqbul Ahmed, the heir of Sirajul Haque, in four annas share, sold 21 decimals of land to the plaintiff No.1 by a registered deed of sale dated 2-1-1963. Jobedullah one of the heirs of recorded co-sharer Idris Mia sold 21 decimals of land to the plaintiff N6.1 by a registered deed of sale dated 31-1-1959. In Plot No.743 of the said Khatian, one Abdul Jalil was the owner of 56 decimals of land by purchase which was acquired by Ayesha by transfer. She was also the owner of 20 decimals of land in Plot No.663 and 73 decimals of land in Plot No.738. Ayesha sold 1.29 acres of land to Jayeda Khatun by different deeds of sale and Jayeda Khatun in her life time sold 1.29 acres of land to the plaintiff No.2 by a registered deed of sale dated 26-2-1959. Thus, the plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 have been owning and possessing 1.15 and 1.29 acres of land respectively, in all, 2.44 acres of land in the said khatian. During last diara operation, the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant Nos.1-3. As a result, the plaintiffs' title to the suit land has been clouded. Hence, the suit has been filed. 

 3. The respondent No.1 herein as added the defendant No.28 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material statements made in the plaint. His case, in short, was that the suit land had gone under the river and because of embankment, the suit land again reappeared as alluvion and diluvion land and, as such, the title of the original owners extinguished creating right and title of the Government in whose name the diara record was correctly prepared and published. The defendant No.28 has been possessing the suit land by taking settlement and paying rent to the Government and in this circumstances, the suit was liable to be dismissed with costs. 

 5. Feeling aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 30-9-1991 passed by the trial Court in Title Suit No.253 of 1983, the defendant-respondent preferred Title Appeal No.107 of 1991 before the Court of learned District Judge, Lakshmipur and it was transferred to the Court of learned Additional District Judge, Lakshmipur who by his judgment and order dated 20-104997 allowed the appeal. 

 6. Against the judgment and order dated 20-10-1997 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Lakshmipur in Title Appeal No.107 of 1991, the plaintiffs-appellants preferred Civil Revision No.1084 of 1998 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule. 

 9. Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the High Court Division committed error as it has failed to consider that the plaintiffs proved their right, title, interest and possession in the suit land by oral and documentary evidence and the appellate Court below committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice as it did not consider the evidence on right, title, interest and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is not tenable in law. He further submits that the High Court Division committed error in not considering that lower appellate court shifted the burden of proof upon the plaintiffs wrongly about alluvion and dilluvion of suit land. There was no such case or evidence on record rather, defendant No. 28 claimed in the written statement that suit land was alluviated and dilluviated, so burden of proof lies upon defendant No. 28 who asserts the fact. The lower appellate court wrongly mere surmise and conjecture found that plaintiffs failed to prove the alluvion and dilluvion and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside. He next submits that the High Court Division failed to consider that the appellate Court below misdirected itself in law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court without reversing its findings. He also submits that the judgment and order of the High Court Division is not well founded as the High Court Division did not consider that the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below is result of non-consideration, misreading and misinterpretation of the evidences on record. He finally submits that only the contesting defendant No.28 who was Tohshilder of local revenue office who created forged, fabricated and antedated documents of lease though he as Government servant was not entitled to get settlement but the High Court Division as well as the appellate Court below failed to consider it and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is not sustainable in law. 

 10. Mrs Qumrunnessa Raffia, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No.1 submits that the appellate Court below is absolutely right in holding that the onus is upon the plaintiffs to prove that the suit land was not alluviated and dilluviated and hence, the High Court Division rightly passed impugned judgment and order. She further submits that the defendant asserted that before the diara survey suit land was dilluviated and subsequently the suit land was alluviated. Hence, the High Court Division rightly discharged the Rule and passed the impugned judgment and order. She next submits that the defendant did not challenge the title of the plaintiffs and their predecessor. The trial Court without going through the evidence on record and without applying its judicial mind came to a wrong and erroneous findings. He finally submits that the plaintiff-appellants are not entitled to have the decree in the suit in view of the provisions of PO 135 of 1972 and, as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

 13. The High Court Division in passing the judgment and order did not consider the judgment of the lower appellate court in accordance with the materials on record. Rather it is divulged that discussed the extraneous matter and discharged the Rule. The appellants submitted photo of the original documents before us through additional paper book dated 23-11-2000 wherein annexed the exhibits-1, 1(Ka), 1(Kha), 1(Ga), 1(Gha), 1(Uma), 1 (Cha), 2, 3, and 3(Ka) from those documents it is proved that the plaintiffs appellant have title in suit properties. The trial court considering those documents decreed the suit. However, the lower appellate court without considering the legal and lawful aspects of the plaintiff's case travel beyond the materials on record and the High Court Division has also failed to discuss the failure of the lower appellate court as a revisional Court. In this case both revisional and appellate Court have failed to rebut the findings of the trial court in the true perspective of law and facts and circumstances of the case. We are of the considered view that both the courts below committed serious error in law discussing the material on record which resulted serious error of law. 

 14. The Learned Advocate of the defendant respondent argued referring PO 135 of 1972 that plaintiff appellant's right, title, and interest extinguished alluvion and delluvion of the suit property. However, it is the case of the contesting defendant respondent who has claimed that he got the suit property from the Government, the facts remain that Government , is the defendant in the suit but did not filed any written statement supporting the contesting defendant's case. The Government even did not contest in the suit claiming facts that suit properties were alluviated and delluviated. At the trial neither Government nor the contesting defendant respondents have submitted any documents supporting the defence case of all uvion and delluvion. Therefore the provision of PO 135 of 1972 does not come to being effect in the facts and circumstances of the case. It is admitted fact that the contesting defendant respondent is none but the employee of Tahsil office who is not a cultivator. In view of such fact it is apparent that he could not get the Government Khas mohal land in view of provision of 54 and 63 if Estate Manual Rules which runs as follows:-

parties:
AKBAR ALI @ MD. AKBAR ALI AND OTHERS
Vs.
REASUDDIN BEING DEAD HIS LEGAL HEIRS 1(A) 
MD. ANWAR HOSSAIN AND OTHERS
full_judgment:
4. Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali along with Mr. Subrata Saha, learned advocates appeared for the petitioner. Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali learned advocate submits that admittedly the petitioners are co-sharers in the suit land and the total quantum of suit land is 48.43 acres which plaintiffs claim is only 0.55 acres of land for which he got decree in preliminary form. He next submits that after allotting the share to the plaintiff vast tract of land remained as residuary shares and out of that some other defendants namely defendant Nos.94, 189, 190, 199, 73, 113, 111 obtained saham regarding 27.64 acres of land by filing an application, even though they did not submit any sorts of documents in support of their claim, but in spite of filing of relevant documents by the petitioner, the Court below did not consider the documents and objection and without adverting the same rejected the objection which caused failure of justice. He next submits that the appellate Court dismissed the appeal citing some technical ground regarding particular date being erroneously mentioned in the memo of appeal which is technical in nature. He next submits that before drawing up final decree the petitioner filed objection and as such it was incumbent upon the trial Court to consider the contents of the written objection and to direct the advocate commissioner to cause inquiry whether the petitioner is entitled to get his claimed saham from the residuary property, but the trial Court without any consideration rejected the same and drew final decree which caused failure of justice. Apart from this petitioner Nos. 2(a) 2(i) filed an application for allotment of saham in respect of 4.04 acres of land in favour of them. 

 5. Mr. M.M. Haque Siddique Rana, learned advocate appearing for the opposite party submits that after preliminary decree, the opposite party filed an application for appointment of advocate commissioner for demarcating his land and accordingly advocate commissioner went to the locality and thereafter allotted specific saham to the plaintiff opposite party and consequently the trial Court has drawn final decree in pursuance of the commissioner's report and as such the present approach of the petitioner for allotting saham to them from residuary property is not sustainable. He next submits that since the petitioner did not contest the suit in spite of service of summons, their share has not been allotted by the Court and as such they are not entitled to get any share by filing belated application. 

 9. Mr. Subrata Saha urged that due to inadvertence supporting documents of title of the petitioner could not be filed and as such the shares regarding 11.75 acres of land should be allotted to the petitioners contending that out of 48.43 acres of land plaintiffs have got .55 acres of land while other defendants have got 27.94 acres of land and even after allotment of saham to the petitioners still Other lands will remain as residuary property. 

 11. On perusal of the decisions as referred by the learned advocate of the opposite party it appears that before final decree any share can be allotted to the co-sharer in spite of his not having contested to the original suit, if he can prove his title and possession over any residuary shares of any partible property but after pronouncement of final decree there is little scope to consider any co-sharer's claim regarding allotment of share out of residuary ejmali property. In the case of Alekjan Bewa and others vs. Alefa Bewa and others reported in 7 ADC 593, Aziz Ahmed and another vs. Khorsheda Begum alias Monwara Begum and others reported in 7 MLR AD 25, Md. Atar Ali Sheikh and others vs. Md. Karam Ali Sheikh and others reported in 11 BLT 44 similar views are reiterated by our apex Court. 

 12. Total partible land is 48.43 acres out of which plaintiffs claim is only 0.55 acres which has been allotted to him by the Advocate Commissioner and accordingly, final decree has been drawn up. Another 27.94 acres of land has been allotted to other defendant from residuary shares. Apart from the allotted shares still there remained residuary property wherefrom the present petitioners are claiming 15.79 acres of land. In the application for allotting saham the petitioner submitted certain photoset copies of the document in support of their claim. On perusal of the documents it appears that those are old and ancient one but its veracity cannot be ascertained because of having not formally proved. But since residuary shares still remains, the genuineness of the documents and other aspects should be investigated without upsetting the share and possession allotted to the plaintiff opposite party as well as the defendant opposite parties to whom specific shares have been allotted as per showing of the Advocate Commissioner. The trial Court can depute the said Advocate who held investigation regarding the suit land allotting the shares to the plaintiff and other defendants and if, the said advocate commissioner is not available or found absent another advocate commissioner can be deputed for considering petitioners claim out of residuary properties. But before that the petitioners are required to submit all title deeds and other required papers in original or in absence of originals by producing certified copies with due explanation thereof, for making proper inquiry regarding the claim of the petitioner and as such final decree passed by the trial Court is required to be set aside as because keeping the final decree intact inquiry cannot be held regarding the title and other aspect of the petitioners claim. 

 13. In the above context, the final decree dated 26.01.1999 passed by learned Assistant Judge, Bhaluka, Maymensingh and the judgment and decree dated 02.8.2001 passed by erstwhile Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Mymensingh are hereby set aside. The shares allotted to the plaintiff-opposite parties and the defendant-opposite parties by the Advocate Commissioners report as well as possession will remain intact. If any further commission is held and after examining and scrutinizing the documents submitted by the petitioners if the petitioners are entitled to get any share from residuary properties it cannot anyway affect the plaintiff opposite parties share and possession as well as the defendant opposite parties share and possession which they have got meanwhile.

full_judgment:
Soumendra Sarker J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 18-8-2015 at the instance of the defendant No. 1-appellant, which was passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 106 of 2015 allowing an application for temporary injunction filed by the plaintiff-respondents under Order XXXIX, rule 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure granting an order of status quo regarding the nature and character and transfer of the suit property as described in the schedule of the application till disposal of the suit. 

 2. The facts relevant for disposal of the appeal in a nut-shell can be stated thus, the present respondent No. 1 as plaintiff instituted a Title Suit being No. 106 of 2015 in the 3rd Court of learned Joint District Judge, Khulna and during pendency of the suit the plaintiff filed an application for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 along with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure contending inter alia that the disputed property appertaining to police station Terokanda under Mouza-Kola consists of eleven SA khatians comprising an area of 8.154 acres of land originally belonged to one Haji Aftabuddin and the father of the plaintiff Atahar Uddin. By amicable partition the father of the plaintiff Atahar Uddin possessed the suit land and subsequently died leaving behind the plaintiff's mother Mohsena Khanam, two daughters, the plaintiff Maliha Malik and Mahfija Malik and one son Ismail Al Malik as legal heirs. The plaintiff and her sister use to reside at Dhaka after their marriage and for that reason to maintain and look after the property they executed a registered am-mokter nama deed in respect of the land on 19-4-2007. The 'Am-mokter' was the mother of the plaintiff. Subsequently, the brother of the plaintiff by another registered am-mokter nama deed dated 16-6-2010 appointed his mother Mohsena Khanom as of his am-mokter for the aforesaid suit jote with regard to his portion of area. The plaintiff came to know that behind the back of him for the land measuring 11.63 acres an am-mokter nama deed has been created by the defendant No.1. After getting the said deed registered the defendant No. 1 tried to change the nature and character of the disputed property and also threatened the plaintiff to transfer the land in favour of third party which constrained the plaintiff to prefer the temporary injunction application. 

 3. Vis-a-vis the contrary case of the defendant-appellant in short is thus, that no collusion or manipulation was done by the defendant or her husband rather the mother of the plaintiff Mohsena Khanom voluntarily did everything within the knowledge of the plaintiff and others. The mother of the plaintiff after becoming am-mokter of her son and daughters by virtue of two am-mokter nama registered deeds transferred the land measuring 5.92 acres in favour of the defendant- appellant by a registered sub-kabala deed dated 20.10.2010 at a consideration of Taka 17,00,000 (Taka seventeen lac). The possession was delivered by the plaintiffs mother in favour of the purchaser defendant No. 1 for her purchased land and specific boundaries were also given for ascertaining the actual location of the land sold by her in favour of the defendant-appellant. After purchase the defendant-appellant is possessing her purchased land having mutation within the knowledge of the plaintiff and others. The plaintiff out of ill motive only to harass the defendant-appellant having no manner of right, title, interest and possession in the aforesaid 5.92 acres of land, on the basis of false allegations filed the original suit and its subsequent application for temporary injunction for restraining the defendant-appellant from her peaceful possession in her purchased land. 

 7. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-appellant submits that the learned court below committed gross illegality in passing the impugned judgment and order which is out and out a non-speaking order and not proper, rather it is wrong and bad-in-law. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned trial court without perusing the facts of the case and the documents produced from the sides of the respective parties on the basis of surmise and conjecture passed the impugned order which is not in accordance with law and the guiding principle of granting temporary injunction not at all followed by the learned court below before passing the impugned order which is as good as an order of injunction. The learned Advocate also submits that the order of status quo which was passed by the learned court below is practically an order of temporary injunction against the defendant-appellant who is possessing her purchased portion of land. The defendant-appellant is a bona fide purchaser with value and the mother of the plaintiff by virtue of registered admitted "am-mokter nama" transferred the land at a consideration of Taka 17,00,000 (Taka seventeen lac) with demarcation in favour of the defendant No.1. The defendant-appellant getting possession of the land used to possess the same peacefully within the knowledge of everybody including the plaintiff herself. The learned Advocate submits that the court below failed to appreciate the proposition of law and the doctrine of Lis pendense has been overlooked by the learned Joint District Judge before passing the impugned judgment and order. The trial Judge in misconception of law committed error in law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice without going into the plaint of Title Suit No. 106 of 2015 which does not disclose that the kabala being No. 1676 of 2010 in favour of the defendant-appellant is forged, but the plaintiff contended that the Power of Attorney being No. 685 of 2007 and 3329 of 2010 on the basis of which the defendant's kabala was registered were not intended to include the suit land but the fact remains that the plaintiff never challenged the said Power of Attorney by virtue of which the kabala deed was executed and registered by her mother in favour of the defendant and thereby the learned trial court is totally misconceived in grasping the factual aspect of the case resulting in an error in the decision in passing the impugned judgment and order. 

 8. As against the aforesaid submissions the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent argued that, it is not the case of the plaintiff that they did not execute and register the am-mokter nama deed in favour of their mother but it is the case of the plaintiff that the plaintiff's mother has no intention to transfer the suit land in favour of the defendant. The learned Advocate further submits that the original suit was instituted by the plaintiff-respondent against the defendant-appellant and others for a declaration that the schedule deed has been obtained by practicing fraud upon the plaintiff and the said deed is collusive, fraudulent and illegal which is not binding upon the plaintiff. Besides this, it is not the case of the plaintiff that the registered am-mokter nama deeds in favour of their mother were forged, collusive or anti-dated. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the court below during passing the impugned judgment and order rightly decided the merit of the application for temporary injunction in favour of the plaintiff and passed the impugned order rightly and, as such, there is no merit in the appeal. 

 9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates and have gone through the original plaint of Title Suit No. 106 of 2015 filed in the 3rd Court of the learned Joint District Judge, Khulna. We have also perused the application for temporary injunction along with the relevant papers including the title document of the defendant-appellant. The fact remains that the defendant-appellant asserted specifically in her written objection and arguments that she is a bonafide purchaser with value from the admitted am-mokter of the plaintiff-respondent. The further case of the defendant is such that the mother of the plaintiff in her sound mind and health executed and registered the sub-kabala deed in favour of the defendant-appellant which have got every binding effect upon the plaintiff and others. 

 10. We have come across from the papers on record that the learned trial Court in the impugned judgment and order held that both the parties to the suit in respect of their respective claim have got a specific case. It was further held by the learned court below that the mother of the plaintiff being am-mokter of the plaintiff and her brother and sisters entered into a deed of transfer in respect of 5.92 acres of land in favour of the defendant No.1. The learned Joint District Judge in the impugned order opined that for proper adjudication into the matter-in-dispute evidence is required. But the fact remains that, the pleadings of the plaintiff which has been incorporated in the contents of the plaint of Title Suit being No. 106 of 2015 does not challenge or dispute the kabala being No. 1676/2010 in favour of the defendant No. 1 and it is not the case of the plaintiff that the title deed of the defendant is forged, fabricated or collusive. It is also evident from the papers on record that the learned Joint District Judge failed to observe and consider that the material facts and the laws relating for disposal of the application for temporary injunction does not provide any such order which may restrain any of the party to the suit in enjoyment of the property by virtue of any deed which is not at all challenged from the side of the applicant of the injunction application. 

 11. On meticulous consideration of the relevant papers it further transpires that the plaintiff-respondent of this case only for simple declaration instituted the original suit and the declaration is with regard to a particular deed described in the schedule of the plaint which is not identical or consistent with the title deed of the defendant-appellant. Hence, from the face of the papers it is apparent that the learned trial court is totally misconceived in realizing the subject matter-in-dispute between the parties as well as the factual aspect of the case and thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision in passing the impugned judgment and order. Apart from this, the order of status quo which has imposed by the learned court below has ignored the principle of "doctrine of Lis pendence" which is simultaneously applicable in respect of both the parties to the suit till disposal of the original suit on merit. 

 13. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 18-8-2015 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 106 of 2015 is hereby set aside.

parties:
Md. Ruhul Amin being dead his heirs Ayesha Amin and others ----- Appellants
Vs.

full_judgment:
3. After filing the miscellaneous case for pre-emption as the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 129 of 1987 in the same Court for declaration that the registered deed of ewaznama dated 18.06.1987 (which was the subject matter of pre-emption) was an out and out sale deed and not an ewajnama. Subsequently the suit and the miscellaneous case having been transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Senbag were renumbered as Title Suit No. 4 of 1995 and Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1995 respectively. 

 4. The pre-emptees contested the suit and the miscellaneous case by filing written statement and written objection respectively contending, inter alia, that the plaintiffs/ the pre-emptors were not co-sharers by inheritance in the case holding and that they (the pre-emptees) were the co-shares in the case holding inasmuch as on 29.01.1985, pre-emptee No.2 acquired 0.03 acre land by a registered deed of ewaznama dated 29.01.1985, from Makhon Lal Das, vendor No. 3. Thereby, he has been exercising his right, title and possession over the said portion of the land as a co-sharer. Vendor Makhon Lal Das and his wife Dipali Rani by a registered deed of ewaznama dated 18.06.1987 exchanged their 3.89½ acres land as described in schedule -'Ka' with 0.058½ acre land of the pre-emptees as described in schedule- 'Kha' to the pre-emption application. There was a tin shed dwelling house with pucca wall over 'Ka' scheduled land which was also sold to the pre-emptees at taka 2,00,000.00. Subsequently, possession of the respective exchanged land was delivered pursuant to the terms of the ewaznama. After exchanged land was delivered pursuant to the terms of the ewaznama. After exchange the locals threatened to kill the vendors who then decided to settle elsewhere and transferred 'Khat scheduled land to defendant No. 3, Most. Amina Khatun, by a registered kabala dated 19.06.1988 at a consideration of taka 2,90,000.00 Virtually, the transfer was made not by a registered kabala but by a registered ewaznama, showing consideration for taka 25,000.00 only instead of the actual valuation prevailed at that time. Therefore, the suit and the miscellaneous case were liable to be dismissed. 

 5. The suit and the miscellaneous case were heard analogously by the learned Assistant judge, Senbag and he, by a common judgment dated 31.08.1996 dismissed the suit and disallowed the miscellaneous case. Against the judgment and the order respectively of the learned Assistant Judge two appeals being Title Appeal No. 184 of 1996 and Miscellaneous Appeal No. 38 of 1996 were filed before the District Judge, Noakhali. Both the appeals were allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now the Joint District Judge) by a common judgment dated 12.01.1998. 

 6. Against the judgment of the Appellate Court, in the title appeal as well as in the miscellaneous appeal, the pre-emptees who were defendants in the suit, filed one revision application before the High Court Division being Civil Revision No. 2159 of 1988 and a Single Bench by the impugned judgment and order made the Rule absolute with the finding that the deed in question was a deed of ewaznama and not a deed of sale. 

 10. Before we proceed to consider the submissions on which leave was granted, we feel it obligatory on our part to dwell upon a point that very much disturbed our mind, namely, that how one revision application could be filed before the High Court Division challenging the judgment and decree passed in the title appeal as well as the judgment and order passed in the miscellaneous appeal. More interesting thing is that in the cause title even the number of the miscellaneous appeal was not mentioned and in case of Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1995, it was written as Other Suit No.1 of 1995. We were a bit perplexed and astonished to see the cause title of the revision application and to be sure what was the actual cases title in the original revision application (in the paper book the Photostat copy of the revision application has been filed), we brought the records of the civil revision from the High Court Division and found the cause title as mentioned in the Photostat copy of the revision application included in paper book and in the original civil revision exactly the same. The cause title reads as follows: 

 Judgment and decree dated 12.01.1998 and 16.01.1998 respectively passed by Subordinate Judge, Court No.2, Noakhali in Title Appeal No. 184 of 1996 and Other Appeal No. 38 of 1996 arises out of Title Suit No.4 of 1995 and other Suit No.1 of 1995 by which learned appellate court allowed the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree dated 31.08.1996 and 10.09.1996 respectively passed by the Assistant Judge Court, Senbag in the above mentioned suits." (the number of the miscellaneous appeal was 38 of 1996) 

 11. The payer in the revision application was couched keeping conformity with the cause title. Be that as it may, we have no hesitation to say that one revision application was not maintainable though the two appeals (the title appeal and the miscellaneous appeal) were disposed of by a common judgment. And the Rule issuing Bench was absolutely in error in entertaining one revision application against the judgment passed in the two appeals and that again with wrong description of the miscellaneous appeal and the miscellaneous case and then in issuing the Rule. The same error has also been committed by the single Bench which heard the revision and disposed the same finally. In the context, it is very pertinent to state that the Single Bench while passing the impugned judgment and order failed to notice that the judgment passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 38 of 1996 setting aside the order of the learned Assistant Judge passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1995 was not at all impugned in the revision application, but in the ordering portion, it stated that "The impugned judgment and decree dated 12.01.1998 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court Noakhali, in Title Appeal No. 184 of 1996 analogously heard with Miscellaneous Appeal No. 04 of 1995 and Miscellaneous Case No. 01 of 1995 (miscellaneous case arose out of the pre-emption application) stand dismissed." Since the judgment and order passed by the Appellate Court in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 38 of 1996 was not at all impugned in the revision that could not be the subject matter of any sort of adjudication in revision. In this regard, it may be stated that the learned Subordinate Judge who disposed the appeals (the title appeal and the miscellaneous appeal) by the common judgment in unequivocal term allowed both the appeals, i.e. decreed the suit and allowed the miscellaneous case. The ordering portion of the Appellate Court reads as follows: 

 The above facts clearly show the total non-application of mind by the High Court Division which is very much unfortunate and disturbing as well. We hope that the Benches, both the Rule issuing Bench and the hearing Bench, shall apply their judicial mined and see whether a revision application is at all in form and the cause title and the prayer of a revision application are properly framed and couched with correct description and number of the suit and the case. Since the defendant-respondents filed one revision application and the same was decided against the plaintiff-per-emptors, they had no option but to file one civil petition for leave to appeal giving rise to this appeal as stated hereinbefore.
