parties:
Motleb Khan and others ------ Petitioners 
Vs
Md Majid Mollah and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
The was Rule issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 25-8-2008 and 31-8-2008 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali in Title Appeal No. 171 of 2006 disallowing the appeal affirming those dated 20-11-2006 and 27-11-2006 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 41 of 2000 should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the original suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession being Title Suit No. 41 of 2000 in the 1st Court of learned Joint District Judge, Patuakhali, contending inter alia that the suit property appertaining to Mouza Kudbar Char under Mirjaganj police station corresponding to CS Khatian No. 145 measuring an area of 4.12 acres of land originally belonged to one Kasem Ali Kha and Kazem Ali Kha. The CS record was correctly prepared in their names. The original owners died issueless and the property devolved upon their cousin Arman Kha. In the CS Khatian No. 142 the land measuring 8.25 acres have been recorded in the name of Arman Kha. At the demise of Arman Kha his three sons namely Ismail Kha, Asmat Kha and Jonab. Ali Kha inherited the property. In the petty settlement Khatian Nos. 108, 140/2 measuring 3.29 acres of land was recorded in the names of three brothers. Ismail Kha died leaving two daughters Jarina and Urful Nessa and two full brothers Asmat and Jonab All Kha. Urful died leaving behind one son, two daughters who are the plaintiff Nos. 41, 42 and 43. The plaintiffs who are 44 in numbers are the heirs and successive heirs of the recorded owners who possess the suit land for more than 12 years without any break. During settlement operation 2.25 acres of land was recorded in the names of the plaintiffs and the rest has been recorded in the names of the defendants. The plaintiffs have got their paternal homestead in the suit property. The defendants have no manner of title, interest and possession over the suit land but on the basis of wrong SA record they denied the title of the plaintiffs which constrained the plaintiffs to institute the original suit. 

 3. The contrary case of the defendant in short is thus that the superior landlord of the plaintiffs' predecessors was MT Brown Estate under Court of Wards and the land of CS Khatian No. 145 was auction purchased by the superior landlord. Beside this the land of CS Khatian No. 142 was also sold in a certificate case and was purchased by the superior landlord. The Court of Wards took possession of the land through court against which the predecessor of the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 139 of 1945 challenging the auction sale which was dismissed for default. Subsequently, the Court of Wards granted settlement in favour of one Jonab Ali by granting 'dakhilas' and those properties have been recorded in the name of the defendants during Revisional Settlement and State Acquisition operation. The land of Petty Settlement Khatian No. 108 was purchased by the government and the government resettled the same in part to the defendants and in part to the plaintiffs. Apart from this, the land of PS Khatian No. 140/2 was auction purchased by government for arrear of rent and the government leased out the same to the predecessor of the defendant Jonab Ali and one Nawab Ali Mia. The further case of the defendants is such that the SA Khatian has been correctly prepared in their names and they had been owning and possessing the suit land after construction of homestead and they have donated 0.30 acres of land in favour of the government for establishment of a 'Hat'. 

 4. The learned trial court after taking evidence from the sides of the respective parties dismissed the suit on contest on 20-11-2006. Being aggrieved the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 171 of 2006 in the Court of learned District Judge, Patuakhali which was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali and the learned lower appellate court by the impugned judgment and decree disallowed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree passed by the trial court. 

 7. The learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that both the courts below in passing the judgment and dismissal decree and in disallowing the appeal committed illegality and irregularity resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocates further submits that none of the courts considered the facts of the case as to the effect that no paper has been filed to substantiate the delivery of possession pursuant to alleged settlement in favour of defendant-opposite parties. There has been total non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning miscarriage of justice. There is no paper from the side of the defendants that MT Brown Estate ever managed the property under the management of court of Wards and there is no evidence to show that the alleged settlement was granted in favour of the defendant by the Court of Wards. Both the Courts below on surmise and conjecture holding the correctness of the alleged settlement and auction purchase committed error of law. Neither the trial court nor the appellate court considered that there is no evidence of annulment and taking possession of the land by the government. Petty Settlement Khatian marked Exhibits-'Ka-3' and 'Ka-4' shows that the government was not the land-lord which is also not considered by the courts below. It was the case of the plaintiffs that Jonab Ali the predecessor of the defendants created the papers of auction and settlement by the act of fraud and forgery which has vitiated the alleged auction and settlement. The learned Advocates also submit that the courts below misdirected themselves on the question of payment of rent which is on the basis of wrong SA Khatian which has no presumptive value of correctness. The courts below also not considered the evidence of the defendant's witness No.6 who has admitted the possession of the plaintiff-petitioners and their homestead. The learned Advocates lastly submit that it is the case of the defendants that they took pattan from the landlord through 'amaldari dakhila' not by kabuliat. The CS khatian is a title document which proves the bona fide of the plain-tiffs and the evidence adduced from the side of the parties not properly assessed by the learned lower appellate court in its true perspective and there is non-reading and misreading of evidence and non-consideration to material facts in disposing the appeal which is violative to the provisions laid down under Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is not sustainable. 

 8. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned counsels of the petitioners the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule submits that the defendants admit the CS Khatian in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor-in-interest They also admit the title of Arman Kha. But the fact remains that MT Brown Estate the superior landlord for arrear of rent auction purchased the suit land. Subsequently, the defendants were granted settlement. The learned Advocates further submits that both the courts below concurrently held that the plaintiffs are not entitled to get the relief as prayed for since they have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit property. The learned Advocates also submit that the plaintiffs to the suit by subsequent amendment of their plaint challenged the settlement and auction purchase of the defendants in their pleadings. Therefore, the onus of proof totally lies upon the plaintiffs to disprove the auction purchase and settlement of the defendants. The plaintiffs during trial of the original suit failed to discharge their onus in proving their pleading. The learned Advocates lastly submits that the plaintiffs have admitted after amending their original plaint that the recent khatians i.e. record of rights has not been prepared in their names but has been prepared in the names of the defendants. Those khatians have been wrongly prepared, which is the case of the plaintiffs and as a result of that the onus of proof is on the plaintiffs to prove that the SA khatian is wrongly prepared in the names of the defendants. The plaintiffs to the suit also alleged that the certificate sale, auction purchase and subsequent settlement taken by the defendants from the auction purchasers are fraudulent, collusive and not acted upon. Therefore, obviously under sections 101 and 103 of the Evidence Act the onus of proof is on the plaintiffs to prove their respective plea i.e. their case which does not lie on the defendants. Even then, the defendants under the provisions of Evidence Act after calling the volume book and necessary papers showing the certificate sale and auction purchase proved their case and after adducing evidence to that effect have proved that the tenancy of the original owners have been extinguished by virtue of auction sale as cited from the side of the defendants. All the documentary evidence has been properly evaluated by both the courts below and all the evidence on records has been properly assessed in its true perspective before arrival at a decision as to the merit of the suit and its subsequent appeal. There is no misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with. 

 10. On perusal of the case record it transpires that during trial of the original suit both the parties adduced evidence in support of their respective pleadings. It is an admitted position that the CS khatian Nos. 142 and 45 corresponding to RS khatian Nos. 108 and 140/2 marked Exhibits-1, 1(Ka), 1(Kha) and l(Ga) stands recorded in the names of Kazem Ali Kha. It is also admitted from the sides of the respective parties that the plaintiffs are the heirs and successive heirs of the CS and PS recorded tenants. It is the specific contention of the contesting defendants that the land of CS khatian Nos. 142 and 145 was put into certificate proceedings being Nos. 149 and 150 of 1933-34 and in that certificate cases the property was put to an auction. The superior landlord MT Brown Estate auction purchased the same which was duly affected on 20-6-1934 AD. In support of this the defendant-opposite parties produced the bainanama of the certificate proceeding marked Exhibit-'Ga' and 'Gha'. Besides this, it is apparent from the face of the records that during pendency of the original suit under the purview of Evidence Act to prove the certified copy of the bainanama the defendants called for the volume books from Patuakhali Sub-registry office. The concerned record-keeper after bringing the volume books proved the same which go on to show that one Poresh Nath Sen, Manager, Court of Wards on behalf of MT Brown Estate auction purchased the land in dispute. It is also evident from the documents on record that the predecessor of the plaintiffs for cancellation of the auction sale instituted a Title Suit being No. 129 of 1945 in the 3rd Court of the then Munsif, Patuakhali. That suit was dismissed for default. For restoration of the suit the plaintiffs to that suit preferred a Miscellaneous Case being No. 264 of 1946 which was also dismissed on 25-7-1946. To substantiate the aforesaid facts the certified copy of the Suit Register was produced which are Exhibit-'Uma' and 'Cha' respectively. It is the concurrent findings and decision of the courts below that the title of the plaintiffs predecessors has been extinguished by virtue of certificate proceeding and auction sale and in this way the plaintiffs having no manner of right, title and interest in the disputed property are not in a position to get the relief sought for. 

 11. It is a fact that the SA record of rights has got no presumptive value of correctness but it would prevail until and unless it is rebutted. While both the parties adduced evidence in support of their pleadings the onus of proof under the ambit of Evidence Act lies on the parties to prove their respective cases as stated in their pleadings. Consulting the case records it is obvious, to note that the primary onus of proof which was upon the defendants was discharged in proving their bonafide but vis-a-vis despite the pleadings of the defendants have been specifically challenged and denied by the plaintiffs by subsequent amendment of their plaint but that onus of proof was not discharged by producing cogent, tangible evidence from the plaintiff's side. Having gone through the records I find that the witnesses produced from the sides of the parties have been properly assessed by the Courts below. The trial court in his observation and findings discussed the testimony of the witnesses and scrutinizing the evidence on records it is noticed that the plaintiff No.  26 Abdul Latif Khan as witness No. 1 tried to establish their case who deposed on behalf of all the plaintiffs. This witness admits in his deposition that the RS and SA khatians stands recorded in the name of the defendants and prior to this despite he denied that their predecessor-in-interest for setting aside the certificate cases instituted a Title Suit being No. 139 of 1944 which was dismissed on 20-6-1946 and against that the Miscellaneous Case No. 246 of 2006 was also dismissed but the fact remains that the documentary evidence which are produced makes it clear that the predecessor of the plaintiffs actually for cancellation of the certificate proceeding instituted the suit but failed. To substantiate the position of the plaintiffs they have adduced two witnesses and consulting their testimony it can be easily held that they have hopelessly failed to prove the plaintiffs title and possession as alleged over the disputed property. They even do not know the disputed property practically. On the contrary, the defendants in support of their case examined 5(five) witnesses. All the witnesses have been thoroughly discussed by the trial court in his observation and findings and I find nothing non-consideration, misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-appreciation of the actual position of law. It is the established principle of Civil Law that the plaintiffs shall have to stand on their own legs and they cannot bank upon their adversary. In the instant suit after consulting evidence I have the reason to incline such a view that the plaintiffs' to the suit have failed to discharge their onus in proving their respective pleadings. 

 12. Consulting the case records it appears that no such material contradiction, omission or perverse findings is noticed by dint of which it can be held that there has been any sort of illegality in deciding the fate of the suit and its subsequent appeal. In our revisional jurisdiction, scope of interference under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is very limited. Only where it is noticed that there has been misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts or the observation and findings is based upon gross misconception of law or otherwise perverse which is contrary to law, evidence and records; only in that case the judgment and decree of the appellate court can be interfered with. In the instant case as I have already discussed earlier, no such material is transpired by which I can draw such interference that the impugned judgment and decree deserve my interference. 

 13. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs, the impugned judgment and decree dated 25-8-2008 and 31-8-2008 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali, in Title Appeal No. 171 of 2006 disallowing the appeal affirming those dated 20-11-2006 and 27-11-2006 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 41 of 2000 is hereby affirmed. 

 14. The order of status quo granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated. 

 Communicate the judgment and order at once and send down the lower Court's records immediately.

parties:
Most. Shamsunnahar and others
Vs.
Abdul Mannan and Others
full_judgment:
2. Short facts relevant for the disposal of the appeal are that one Chand Mia, predecessor-in-interest of the appellants, instituted Title Suit No.53 of 1990 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge seeking rectification of a deed and declaration of title in respect of the third schedule land claiming that he was the owner of the suit land on the basis of four deeds and the Khatian was also prepared in his name. Subsequently, he sold the second schedule land measuring an area of 0028 decimals to the defendants by registered kabala dated 10th December, 1965. Thereafter, the defendants attempted to encroach into the plaintiffs land when they disclosed that they had purchased the suit land measuring 05 decimals by the said deed. The plaintiff thereupon obtained a copy of the deed and came to know that the defendants fraudulently included 03 decimals more land in the schedule of the deed although he sold only 0028 decimals. He claimed that he did not sell 05 decimals of land to the defendants and that the deed so far as it relates to the excess area of land was forged, which was required to be rectified. 

 4. The trial Court dismissed the suit. On appeal by the plaintiff being Title Appeal No.97 of 1996, the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Sylhet who heard the said appeal reversed the judgment of the trial Court and decreed the suit. The Single Bench of the High Court Division, however, in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction against the said judgment and order of the Court of appeal below, set aside the judgment of the Court of appeal below and restored those of the trial Court. In the plaint the plaintiff sought the following reliefs: 

 5. According to the plaintiff he sold 0028 decimals of land but the defendants fraudulently included 003 decimals of land in the impugned deed in collusion with the scribe. The plaintiff did not deny the execution of the disputed deed. Besides claiming title, the plaintiff sought for rectification of the impugned deed under section 31 of the Specific Relief Act. The Court of appeal below as well as the High Court Division totally confused as to the nature of the suit the plaintiff was required to file for the relief. The Court of appeal below was of the view that the plaintiff was entitled to a relief under section 31 and accordingly decreed the suit. The High Court Division, on the other hand, is of the opinion that the suit for rectification of the deed is maintainable subject to the condition that the plaintiff is required to prove that the instrument was obtained through fraud or by mutual mistake of the parties. The plaintiff did not seek for cancellation of the entire deed, and under such circumstances, it was incumbent for him to seek the relief under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, praying for a declaration that the deed in Question so far as it relates to inclusion of 0028 decimals of land is void. 

 7. To establish a case of rectification of an instrument, it is required to prove that there has been either fraud or common mistake. The plaintiff does not claim that 05 decimals of land have been mentioned in the deed due to common mistake or through inadvertence. In case of the rectification of a deed, the Court will amend the language of the instrument for the purpose of making it accord with the true intention of the parties, having ascertained what that intention was. In most cases of rectification, the proximate origin of mistake lies in the carelessness or want of skill of the draftsman, but if, one of the parties to conceal some fact does not wish to disclose that has caused the instrument to be so framed as to defeat the intention known to himself, the cases of this kind are likely to be on the verge of fraud. Therefore, in case of rectification of an instrument it must be proved that it was through a mutual mistake of the parties that instrument in question did not truly express the intention of the parties and the Court is required to see that there has been mistake in framing the instrument and also ascertain the real intention of the parties executing it. If these two elements are satisfied, it is in the discretion of Court to grant rectification. 

 9. In case of cancellation of an instrument, three conditions are requisite for the exercise of jurisdiction: (i) the instrument is void or voidable against the plaintiff (ii) the plaintiff may reasonably apprehend serious injury by the instrument being left outstanding and (iii) in the circumstances of the case the Court considers it proper to grant relief of preventive justice. Relief as to cancellation of instrument is founded upon  administration of protective justice for fear that the instrument may be vexatiously or injuriously used by the defendant against the plaintiff when the evidence to impeach it may be lost. When the plaintiff seeks to establish title in himself and cannot establish that title without removing insuperable obstruction such as, an instrument to which he has been party, then he must get that the instrument cancelled and his suit is for cancellation of the instrument. 

 10. The Court of appeal below accepted the argument of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff that it was not a believable story that the plaintiff sold .05 acre of land in Sylhet Municipality area at a consideration of Tk. 95, that the findings of the trial Court regarding the price of the suit land was not acceptable and that since the plaintiff proved his title by adducing documentary evidence, he was not required to prove title by oral evidence. These observations are based on hypothesis, firstly, because the plaintiff failed to prove by adducing documentary evidence that the price of .05 acre of land during the relevant time was much higher, secondly, when the recitals in the admitted deed clearly disclosed the price of the land sold at Tk. 95/- oral evidence varying the recitals in the deed is not admissible and thirdly, the appellate Court declared tie plaintiffs title of the suit land relying on documentary evidence without ascertaining possession in failing to consider that the plaintiff being the original owner it was natural that he had in his possession the original deeds of title but the crux of the matter was whether the defendants got possession of the land covered by the Impugned deed and whether the deed was acted upon. The trial Court on assessment of the evidence came to a definite finding that the defendants are in possession since the date of execution of the deed on 10th December, 1965, so the deed has acted upon. The appellate Court did not reverse the finding of possession.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 16-4-2006 passed in Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 by the learned District Judge, Dhaka dismissing the revisional application by the petitioners and affirming the judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 by the Assistant judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka allowing the application of the defendants under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure by setting aside the judgment and ex parte decree dated 23-6-99 and restoring the Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 in its original file and number should not be set aside. 

 2. The petitioners as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 215 of 1996 in the Court of Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka subsequently transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Nawabganj and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession against the defendant-opposite parties stating, inter alia, that the suit property being homestead property belong to Hanif Sarker, who transferred the same by a registered sale deed dated 12-2-1964 in favour of the mother of the plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 1-2. The defendant Nos. 1-2 were allowed to live in the said homestead as licensee or with permission. The mother of the plaintiffs gifted the suit property and delivered the possession of the same to the plaintiffs by an oral gift dated 17-9-92. The defendant Nos. 1-2 obtained permission from the plaintiffs to live therein as licensee as before. Thereafter the mother of the plaintiffs swore an affidavit before the Notary Public, Dhaka in respect of her earlier oral gift in favour of the plaintiffs. That other two brothers namely, Kabir and Humayun of the plaintiffs were the witness in the said affidavit and the plaintiffs are in possession of some portion of the suit land through their tenant. That the plaintiffs served a notice upon the defendants to vacate the suit premises but the defendants declined to do so, hence the instant suit. 

 4. The defendant-opposite party No. 2 Md Mizanur Rahman filed on application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the aforesaid ex parte decree and the above application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 35 of 1999 and at the same time he preferred a Title Appeal being No. 769 of 1989 before the District Judge, Dhaka against the judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka. 

 5. Thereafter, the aforesaid Title Appeal No. 769 of 1999 was allowed by the District Judge by his judgment and decree dated 29-3-2001 by setting aside the District Judge by his judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka and sent back the suit on remand for further hearing. 

 6. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 29-3-2001 passed in Title Appeal No. 769 of 1999 the plaintiff-petitioners preferred a Civil Revision No. 3834 of 2001 before the High Court Division and obtained the Rule and ultimately the High Court Division was pleased to make the Rule absolute by their judgment and decree dated 8-1-2002 and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court (District Judge). 

 9. In the meantime, defendant-opposite party No.1 filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the trial Court on 20-2-2000 and the same was rejected as Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 for setting aside the judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka. On the other hand, the plaintiff-petitioners filed a Title Execution Case No. 4 of 2000 before the Court of Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka. 

 10. The defendant-opposite party No. 1 appeared in the aforesaid execution case and filed an application for stay of all further proceedings of the Title Execution Case No. 4 of 2000 till disposal of the Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 and the plaintiff-petitioners-filed a written objection against the said application for stay and after hearing the Executing Court was pleased to reject the same on 30-10-2003 and the defendant-opposite party No. 1 was evicted from the suit land and possession of the property was handed over to the plaintiff-petitioners on 30-11-2003 at 2-30 PM through bailiff. 

 11. The defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-2 threatened the plaintiff-petitioner No. 3 and compelled her to file different applications on 20-3-2005 and give deposition before the trial Court for allowing the Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 for setting aside the judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 passed by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka and in order to save her life she did the same which was not done voluntarily but under the threat and coercion of defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 which did not carry any value in the eye of law. 

 12. That the above Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 was heard on 23-3-2005 and the trial Court was pleased to allow the same by his judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 and restored the Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 to its original file and number after setting aside the ex parte decree dated 23-6-99. 

 13. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka allowing the case setting aside the judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 the plaintiff-petitioners preferred a Civil Prevision No. 262 of 2005 before the District Judge, Dhaka. 

 18. Thereafter on 19-3-2006 the plaintiff-petitioners and the defendant-opposite party No. 1 jointly filed an application for re-calling the order dated 22-11-2005 and 30-11-2005 for restoring the order dated 5-10-2005 and the learned District Judge, Dhaka allowed the application and restored the Civil Revision to its original file and number and fixed the date on 4-4-2006 for hearing of solenama. Thereafter the learned District Judge, Dhaka after hearing the Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 was pleased to reject the same without disposing the solenama filed by the parties by his judgment and order dated 16-4-2006 and thereby committed an error of law resulting an error in decision occasioning failure of justice. On receiving the judgment and order dated 16-4-2006 passed in Civil Revision No. 262 by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, the learned Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 4 of 2000 filed by the plaintiff-petitioners on 9-5-2006 passed an order to issue writ for delivery of possession of the suit land in favour of the defendant-opposite party No. 1 and on the basis of the aforesaid order the defendant-opposite parties are trying to dispossess the vendee of the plaintiff-petitioners. 

 20. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order dated 16-4-2006 passed in Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 by the learned District Judge, Dhaka dismissing the revisional application and affirming the judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka allowing the application of the defendant-opposite party No. 1 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure by setting aside the judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 the plaintiff-petitioners preferred the instant revisional application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule. 

 21. The learned Counsel Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan with Mr Syed Mokkadas Ali, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners at the very outset of the hearing draws my attention to the order dated 23-3-2005 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 for revival of ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 and submits that in the context of the judgment passed by the highest judicial forum of Supreme Court, Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1413 of 2002 the learned Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka is absolutely wrong and committed gross illegality by entertaining the application for revival of Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 since the matter has already been decided by the Appellate Division. Next he submits that thereafter the plaintiff preferred a revisional application before the learned District Judge, Dhaka being Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005. The learned District Judge, Dhaka after hearing the revision passed the order on 5-10-2005 stating that since both the parties jointly filed the solenama the revisional application was allowed and the order dated 23-3-2005 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 was set aside. Thereafter the defendant No. 2 Mizanur Rahman behind the back of the plaintiff filed an application on 9-11-2005 and prayed for stay operation of the order dated 5-10-2005, the learned District Judge, Dhaka fixed the date for hearing of the application on 15-11-2005. Thereafter on 10-11-2005 defendant No. 2-opposite party submitted another application stating, inter alia, that the copy of the application dated 9-11-2005 has been served upon the lawyer of the petitioner as such the date of hearing of the stay petition may kindly be heard expeditiously and the learned District Judge, Dhaka was pleased to hear the stay petition on the same day and allowed the petition stating that the order passed by him on 5-10-2005 has been stayed till 15-11-2005. Thereafter on 15-11-2005 opposite party No. 1 Abul Fayez Abdullah also appeared and submitted a petition for stay operation of the order dated 5-10-2005 and disposed of the matter after hearing both the parties. Hearing the opposite party Nos. 1-2 the learned District Judge, Dhaka fixed the date of hearing for stay petition and also to cancel the solenama fixed the date on 21-11-2005 and the order of stay extended up to that date. On 16-11-2005 opposite party No. 1 submitted another application for early hearing of the stay petition preferably on that date instead of 21-11-2005 because the copy of the petition has already been served upon the petitioner and the learned District Judge, Dhaka partly allowed the prayer and fixed the date for hearing of the stay petition on 17-11-2005. On 17-11-2005 opposite party Nos. 1-2 filed Hazira for hearing of the stay petition but the petitioner was not present in the Court. Since the learned Presiding Judge was on leave the hearing of the stay petition fixed on 22-11-2005. It appears from the order-sheet on 22-11-2005 opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 filed Hazira and the record was taken up for hearing and after hearing the stay petition the learned District Judge, Dhaka set aside the order dated 5-10-2005 passed by him earlier in Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 and fixed the date for hearing of the revision on 30-11-2005. Thereafter on 30-11-2005 since the petitioner of the revision was not present and on the other hand, the opposite party Nos. 1-2 remains present in the Court by filing Hazira, the learned District Judge, Dhaka took up the matter for hearing and the revision was dismissed for default. Thereafter on 31-1-2006 the petitioner filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure stating that the opposite party Nos. 1-2 behind the back of the petitioner by practicing fraud upon the Court and obtained an order on 22-11-2005 and 30-11-2005 canceling the earlier order dated 5-10-2005 and prayed for restoration of order dated 5-10-2005 and the date was fixed on 23-2-2006 for hearing of the application. Subsequently the opposite party No. 2 on 15-3-2006 filed a written objection against the application filed by the petitioner under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and prayed for time and the time was allowed and the date was fixed on 19-3-2006 for hearing of the petition. Thereafter on 19-3-2006 both the petitioner and the opposite party Nos. 1-3 jointly filed an application to the effect that the application filed by the petitioner dated on 31-1-2006 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to cancelled the order dated 22-11-2005 and 30-11-2005 for restoration of the order dated 5-10-2005 along with solenama be restored. The learned District Judge, Dhaka allowed the application under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and cancel the order dated 30-11-2005 and restored the Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 and fixed the date for hearing on 4-4-2006. Thereafter on 4-4-2006 opposite party No. 1 prayed for adjournment of the case and next date was fixed on 9-4-2006. Thereafter on 12-4-2006 the learned District Judge, Dhaka heard the Civil Revision No. 262 of 2004 and fixed the date on 16-4-2006 for order. On 16-4-2006 the learned District Judge, Dhaka dismissed the revision and affirmed the order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 and thereby set aside the ex parte judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 restoring the original suit to its original file and number. The learned Counsel Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan finally, submits that the learned District Judge, Dhaka acted illegally and committed error occasioning failure of justice because he cannot set aside his own order after signing the order finally he has become functus officio. The learned District Judge, Dhaka ought to have considered that in this checkered backdrop of the case, particularly where the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in their finding and decision in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1413 of 2002 in respect of the Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 rejected the leave petition filed by the opposite parties. The learned District Judge, Dhaka ignoring the decision and finding of the Appellate Division and his own order passed on 5-10-20005 which was absolutely wrong and fallacious and liable to be interfered by this Court. 

 24. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case and the discussion made above I find substance in the submission of the learned Counsel Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan for the plaintiff-petitioners. Hence the judgment and order dated 16-4-2006 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, in Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 dismissing the revisional application and affirming the judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 by the learned Assistant Judge Nawabgonj, Dhaka, allowing the application of defendants Under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure by setting aside judgment and ex parte decree dated 23-6-1999 and restoring the Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 its original file and number is hereby set aside.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 797 of 2005
parties:
Md. Fazlur Rahman and others ------ Defendant-Petitioners
Vs.
Haji Md. Manir Khan and others ------ Plaintiff-Respondents
full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim J.: This petition for Leave to Appeal at the instance of the defendant-petitioner is directed against the judgment and order dated 16.04.2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3780 of 2000 discharging the Rule affirming the judgment and decree dated 13.08.1998 passed by the Additional Judge, Anti-Smuggling Tribunal, Sylhet in Title Appeal No. 103 of 1997 dismissing the appeal affirming those dated 19.02.1997 passed by the Second Additional Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 8 of 1978. 

 2. The predecessor of the respondents as plaintiff on 12.09.1973 filed the Title Suit No. 223 of 1973 (renumbered as Title Suit No. 8 of 1978) before the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet for declaration title in the suit land in schedule and confirmation of possession in respect of land described in schedule II and for recovery of khas possession in respect of lands described in schedule III. 

 3. The case of the plaintiff-respondents, in brief, is that the suit land originally belonged to Ramesh Chandra Chowdhury, Ransil Chandra Chowdhury and Suresh Chandra Chowdhury who died leaving behind only son Sankar Prasad Chowdhury, the pro-forma defendants Nos. 13 and 14, entered into an agreement for sale with the plaintiff for the suit land with a consideration of Tk. 15,000.00 and executed a Bainapatra on 14.04.1969 in favour of the plaintiff on receipt of Tk. 13,000.00 and delivered possession thereof and they agreed to execute the requisite kabala within three months on receipt of balance consideration, but on being refused the original plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 202 of 1969 for specific performance of contract against the pro-forma defendant Nos.13 and 14 and got decree on 26.01.1970 and also got the kabala on 11.02.1972 through Court vide Title Execution Case No. 5 of 1970. That defendant Nos. 1-3, 9-12 and predecessor of defendant Nos. 4-8 created some false, fraud, fraudulent, collusive and anti-dated documents by false personification. The aforesaid defendants wrongfully and forcefully dispossessed the plaintiffs on 06.09.1972 from the suit 3rd schedule land and also threatened to dispossess from the 2nd schedule land and hence the suit. 

 5. The further case of the defendant-petitioner is that Subrata and Shuhendu, son of Suresh Chowdhury, contracted to sell dag No. 2283 of the 2nd schedule land with defendant Nos. 1 and 2 on 10.04.1964 and delivered possession thereof. That the defendant took settlement in 1358 B.S of the suit 3rd schedule land from the Zaminder Romesh Chandra Chowdhury and Suresh Chandra Chowdhury and since then was possessing the same living therein with their families. That as the record of right wrongly prepared in the name of Ex-landlord, this defendant filed Title Suit No. 150 of 1969 in the first Court of Munsif, Sylhet for correction of the record of right; that the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 202 of 1969 was not binding upon this defendant as he was not a party to the suit and that the plaintiff had no right, title interest over the suit land and hence prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 6. Mr. M.A. Gaffar, learned Advocate, for the petitioner submits that the High Court Division while passing the impugned judgment and order did not appreciate the submission made by the learned Advocate of the petitioner that both the Courts below have failed to take into account that the plaintiffs claim in the suit land is based upon a Bainapatra on the basis of which he obtained an ex-parte decree in Title Suit No. 202 of 1969 wherein the predecessor of the petitioners was not a party and only on the strength of the ex-parte decree the plaintiffs were not entitled to any decree in the subsequent Title Suit No. 8 of 1978 without producing the Bainaptra and without proving the genuineness of the said Bainapatra in the subsequent suit within the meaning of Section 101 of the Evidence Act. 

 8. Mr. Gaffar furthers submits that all the Courts below including the High Court Division have failed to consider the submission   of the learned Advocate of the petitioners that the exparte judgment and decree passed in T.S. No. 202 of 1969 on the basis of which subsequent degree in Title Suit No. 8 of 1978 was passed in not binding upon the defendant No. 1 as he was not a party to that suit; that all the Courts below misconstrued the documentary evidences in order to disbelieve the case of the defendant No.1. 

 9. The plaintiff-respondent examined 4 witnesses in support of his case and filed documents which were marked Exhibit-1 to Exhibit-7 and the same were admitted without objection. The defendant-appellants as well examined 4 witnesses and produced Exhibit-A to Exhibit-C. The defendant though objected before the trial Court to the effect that the Suresh Chandra Chowdhury had no son named Sanker Prashad Chowdhury but has obtain exparte decree in the Title Suit No. 202 o 1969 that they had no absolute right, interest and possession in the suit land and the trial Court has held that there is evident that Suresh Chandra Chowdhury had a so named Sanker Prashad Chowdhury and has been possessing the suit land. The trial Court also decreed the suit holding that on 06.09.1972 the defendants have dispossessed the plaintiff from the Schedule land. The fact of Sanker Prasha Chwodhury being a son of Suresh Chandra Chowdhury has been proved by PW-1 {Exhibit-1,2,3,3(a)}. The fact to the alleged dispossession the plaintiff has sought to prove that the plaintiff was dispossessed on 06.09.1972 from the Schedule-3 land of the suit. Fact remain that though the defendant claims the sin land but they have not challenged the decree in Title Suit No. 202 of 1969 at the proceeding in Execution No. 5 of 1970. On the contrary the defendant No.1 ha failed to prove the alleged patta, kabala deed dated 03.06.1972 and unregister bainanama dated 10.04.1969 being the basis of his alleged possession and title the suit land and thus failed to prove the same.

2. It appears from the order that the appellants filed a suit being Title Suit No. 265 of 1998. This suit was fixed for hearing on 21.07.1999 but in the absence of the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs the suit was dismissed for default. 

 6. Mr. A.K.M. Salahuddin Khan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the original suit being Title Suit No. 197 of 1997 was filed in the Fifth Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, which was subsequently transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Additional Artha Rin Court No. 1, Motijheel, Dhaka, and re-renumbered as the Title Suit No. 265 of 1998. He submits that this Artha Ain Court is situated at Motijheel, Dhaka, about 3 miles away from the premises at Dhaka District Judge's Court, that on the relevant date on 21.07.1999, the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs, after arguing a case being Title Suit No. 13 of 1998, in the Fourth Court of Artha Rin Adalat, situated in the original premises of the Dhaka District Judge's Court rushed to Motijheel for appearing in the instant suit there but due to traffic jam he could not make it in time and consequently the suit was dismissed for default, that immediately after arriving in the Court at Motijheel, the teamed Advocate filed an application for recalling the order of dismissal of the suit but the said petition was rejected, that subsequently on 04.08.1999 he filed another application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, renewing his prayer for re-calling the order of dismissal but the said petition was also rejected. Thereafter the appellant filed the miscellaneous case on 09.08.1999, praying for restoration of the suit but that was also dismissed on contest. 

 7. The learned Advocate for the appellants submits that on the date of the hearing the plaintiff no.2 himself was present in the Court but due to temporary absence of his learned Advocate, the suit was dismissed for no fault of the plaintiffs that in the miscellaneous case also the plaintiff no. 2 examined himself in support of the case. He lastly submits that it was not the fault of the plaintiffs, rather, his learned Advocate after attending the Court in the original premises at Dhaka District Judge's Court could not reach the Court situated at Mali jheel in time because of traffic jam, beyond his control and there by he was prevented by sufficient cause for non appearance before the Court when the said suit was taken up for hearing, that after reaching there, he immediately filed an application at 12-50 p. m. praying for recalling the order of dismissal which showed his diligence in the matter. 

 10. Mr. A. K. M. Salauhddin Khan, the learned advocate submits that he was all along very vigilant to reach the court which is situated about 3 miles away from the original premises of the Dhaka District Judge's Court because of traffic jam. He however, could reach the court at Motijheel at about 12.40 p. m. after completing his arguments in another Court at 11.30 a.m. situated at Dhaka District Judges Court premises. This explanation for his delay ought to have considered by the learned Judge. In a miscellaneous case filed under Order IX rule 9 of the Code the only issue before the Court is as to whether there was sufficient grounds for non-appearance of the plaintiff or his learned Advocate. But the learned Judge did not consider this issue at all, rather, he considered the earlier adjournments of hearing of the suit on the prayers made on behalf of the plaintiffs which is only secondary and can only be considered after his finding on the non-appearance of the plaintiffs on the relevant date. There he committed the error of law. Besides, the learned Advocate explained that due to traffic jam in the rush hour, he was delayed in coming from the premises of the Dhaka District Judge's court to the Court of the Artha Rin Adalat, situated at Motijheel, 3 miles away. This explanation of traffic jam from the old Dhaka area where the District Judges Court's are situated to Motijheel Commercial area during rush hour, is common knowledge. 

 13. In the result the appeal is allowed without any order as to casts. The suit is restored to its original file and number. It appears that the suit is long pending since 1997. The learned Judge is directed to dispose of the suit within the period of one year from the date of receipt of this judgment and order. Send down the lower Court records at once.

2. The respondent No.1 filed the above writ petition calling in question the judgment and order dated 10.11.93 passed by the 1st Court of Settlement, Dhaka in Settlement Case No.10 of 1988 by which the enlisting of House No. 11/5, Block-F Joint Quarter, Mohammadpur, Dhaka in the "Ka" list of the abandoned building, was upheld. In the writ petition it was stated, inter alia, that the above building was allotted to Md. Shafi by a registered lease deed dated 19.4.62; while in peaceful possession of the building Md. Shah, on 08.01.1970 entered into an agreement with the respondant No.1 for sale of the building at a total consideration of Tk.9,750/- out of which the respondent No.1, paid to Md. Shafi a sum of Tk.7,000/- as earnest money and on the same very day Md. Shafi handed over possession of the said building to him; Md. Shafi did not comply with his part of the contract though the respondent No.1 complied with his part of the contract and so he filed Title Suit No. 138 of 1976 against. Md. Shafi seeking specific performance of the contract in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) Dhaka and he after obtaining decree on 26.6.78 put the said decree in execution by filing a Title Execution Case No. 37 of 1978 and got the sale deed executed and registered in his favour; the Government then filed Miscellaneous Case No. 248 of 1986 under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting aside the aforesaid ex-parte decree which was allowed on condition that the Government will pay Tk.30,000/and in case of default the said miscellaneous case shall stand dismissed; the Government having failed to comply with the said condition the miscellaneous case stood dismissed for default; the respondent No.1 had been in possession of the disputed building since the date of agreement dated 8.1.70 and being in possession he got his name mutated and has been paying municipal taxes and other bills but even then above building was listed as an abandoned property by the Gazette Notification published on 23.9.86; the Court of Settlement by judgment and order 10.11.93 dismissed the above case. The respondent No. t of the writ petition, who is the appellant herein, contested the said writ petition without filing any affidavit-in-opposition. The High Court Division after hearing made the Rule absolute. 

 3. Leave was granted to consider the submissions that the High Court. Division not being the court of appeal erred in law in interfering with the findings of fact arrived at by the Court of Settlement and that during the relevant period the whereabouts of the original owner of the above building not being known and the said original owner also having failed to look after and possess 

 4. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant submits that the High Court Division not being the court of appeal, can not interfere with the findings of fact arrived by the Court of Settlement which is the final authority to decide the character of the property; the decree for specific performance of contract and the deed of sale pursuant to the said decree being hit by the provisions of P.O. 16 of 1972 the High Court Division erred in law in making the rule absolute; the whereabouts of the original owner not being known during the relevant period and the original owner having failed to look after and possess the above building personally at the relevant time the Court of Settlement rightly held that the above building duly vested to the government; the High Court Division erred in law in shifting the onus on the Government to prove that the property was an abandoned property specially when the enlisting and publication of the said building in the Gazette Notification published on 23.09.1986 conclusive proof of its abandoned character. 

 5. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent No.1 on the other handed submits that the Government, the appellant herein, did never serve any notice either upon the respondent No.1 or upon the original owner of the building for surrendering their possession declaring the building as abandoned properly and there was also no material before the Court of Settlement to show that the possession of the building has been taken over by the appellant at any time in compliance of section 5(1) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 or P.O. No. 16 of 1972 and further the respondent No.1 along with his vendor, was also in physical possession of the building and was never dispossessed from the building and stilt is in possession of the same on mutating his name in the Government Khatian and has been paying municipal taxes, gas bills and so the decision of the High Court Division does not call for any interference 

 6. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute holding as follows: "On perusal of the Judgment of the Court of Settlement we find that while disposing the petition of the writ petitioner it compared the signature of the Vendor appearing in the original lease deed with the signature of agreement of sale as if deciding the Title of the parties. The Court of Settlement without considering the basic aspect of that is to see as to whether the property is an abandoned property under the provision of P.0.16 of 1972 and whether the soil property under the provision of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. It appears that the respondent Government appearing before the Court of Settlement could not produce any materials to show that the original allottee being a non-local did anything prejudicial to the war of liberation of Bangladesh. There is also no material before the court of Settlement that the possession of the property was taken by the Government under Section 5(1) of the Ordinance No.54 of 1985. The court of Settlement is not a Civil Court to decide title". 

 7. However, as it appears the Court of Settlement found that the respondent No.1 did not possess the vital documents of title i.e. the original allotment letter dated 16.9.1961, registered lease agreement dated 19.4.1963 and letter of delivery of possession dated 26.6.62. Before the Court of Settlement the learned lawyer for the respondent No.1 tried to meet the said position by contending that at the time of execution of the agreement for sale the original owner supplied to the respondent No.1 merely the photostat copies of the aforesaid documents but the Court of Settlement did not accept the above contention as at the relevant time i.e. in the year 1970, there was no photostat machine in the country and moreover on perusal of the said photostat copies the Court of Settlement found that those were made from the office Copies and Duplicate Registered Lease Agreement preserved in the office-file of the Deputy Commissioner of Housing and Settlement Department and the photostat copies filed by the respondent No.1 contained the words "0/C" and "Duplicate" and further the note dated 27.09.83 at para-4 of the page-2 of the file of the above building supports this and the respondent No.1 also submitted the Photostat copy of the 1st page of the same file. Moreover on perusal of the aforesaid office file the Court of Settlement found that Md. Shafi signed each and every document in English including the registered lease deed whereas he executed the alleged bainanama in Urdu which made the Court of Settlement to hold that the alleged bainanama is a forged and anti-dated and the respondent No.1, thus obtained the exparte decree on the basis of the same and further there is no evidence that Md. Shafin was present in Bangladesh after the,25th March, 1971 and moreover till the date of judgment i.e. 10.11.1993, there was also no trace of him. 

 8. It further appears that the scope of certiorari applying which the High Court Division made the Rule absolute is very limited and moreover the High Court Division did not advert to the finding of the Court of Settlement regarding absence of original documents and the absence of Md. Shafi in the Bangladesh after 25th March 1971. So the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division cannot be sustained.

The principal opposite party Nos. 1-4 filed Title Suit No. 8 of 1989 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Keraniganj Upazila praying for declaration that the plaintiffs got right, title and possession in the suit property, that the registered sale deed No. 15892 dated 6-10-1983 in favour of the defendant No. 1 petitioner executed and registered through Court is illegal, void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiffs and also that the Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1984 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Keraniganj is illegal, without jurisdiction as being not in consonance with its original suit being Title Suit No. 306 of 1969.

This petitioner as defendant No. 1 has been contesting the suit by filing written statement stating, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable, that the suit is barred by the principle of res-judicata. The further case of the petitioner is that the opposite party No. 5 while owning and possessing the suit property entered into an agreement with petitioner on 1-1-1969 to sell the same and subsequently the petitioner got the specific performance of the said contract in the Title Suit No. 3(16 of 1969 and got the Kabala Deed No. 15892 dated 6-10-1983 registered through Court vide Title Execution Case No. 21 of 1981 and obtained possession of the suit property (in part) vide Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1984 (renumbered on transfer) and was waiting for obtaining possession of the rest of the suit property. Md. Idris alias Shelim & ors ------ Petitioners 
vs.
Bazal Ahmed & ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
4. Mr. Nirmalendu Bikash Dutta, the learned Advocate, placed before me the application for adding the petitioner as co-plaintiff in the aforesaid suit. From perusal of the petition it seems that the petitioner claimed title in the suit premises on the basis of a gift by the original owner in favour of one Mustafizur Rahman. On the other hand, the claim of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 is on the basis of ex-change by heirs of Abul Hossain and Noor Hossain who were the uncle of the petitioner. It also appears from the records that the petitioner has instituted D.C. Suit No. 51 of 1986 in the court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong against the opposite party No. 1 for declaration that the deed of exchange was void collusive, fraudulent. Thus from the facts it appears as stated above that there is a conflict of claims over title in the suit premises. As the applicant has got basis of his claim in the suit premises I hold that he is a necessary party in the present suit in as much as the issues can be settled between the plaintiff and the applicant effectively and completely. This conclusion of mine gives rise to other questions. Whether he will be added as co- applicant or defendant in the suit. If the applicant is added as co-plaintiff in that case the necessary issue, the conflicting claims as to title, can not be framed and will remain undecided. But if the applicant is added as defendant the issue on title can be framed and decided between the plaintiff and applicant. 

 5. Mr. Dutta also submits that as the applicant has put forward a conflicting claims with the plaintiff the applicant cannot be added as co-plaintiff in that the necessary issue could not be framed for decision for deciding the title in between the original plaintiff and added co-plaintiff. Mr. Dutta refers me to the case of Ram Gopal Sah Vs. Dhirendra Nath and another, 1981 Pat. 298. In that case somewhat similar situation arose. One Shiva Narayan Sah instituted a title Suit for eviction of one Dhirendranath Dey from a house. On the death of Shiva Narayan Sah his son Ramgopal Sah filed an application for substitution as plaintiff in place of his father which was allowed Thereafter one Bimli Devi prayed for substitution in place of the original plaintiff Shib Narayan claiming herself to be the sole surviving heir as widow. The said petition was filed out of time followed by an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act for condo nation of delay. The court rejected the application for substitution on the ground of limitation. Thereafter, Bimli Devi filed an application in the suit under Order 1 Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure for being added as co- plaintiff on the ground that she was the widow of the original plaintiff Shiva Narayan Shah. But the court by an order directed Bimli Devi to be added as plaintiff No. 2 on contest. 

 "............ where the plaintiff disputed the right of a party to have an interest in the property which the plaintiff was claiming, that party should be properly joined as a defendant and not as a co-plaintiff, because if he was joined as a defendant, an issue could be raised between the plaintiff and the party newly joined. This seems to be really the principle underlying a party being joined to the suit in a case like the present. It is only if he is joined as a defendant that an issue can be legitimately raised between him and the plaintiff, when the plaintiff disputes the title of the party applying to be made a party to the suit." 

 7. As in the instant case it appears that the applicant put forward a conflicting claim of title in the disputed premises, on the strength of the aforesaid decision, I hold that where a party seeks to be added as a co-plaintiff in a suit and puts forward conflicting claim as to title of the property in dispute he should not be allowed to be added as a co-plaintiff but he can be made defendant in the suit for the purpose of effective and complete adjudication of issue which may be raised for decision in between the plaintiff  and the added defendant. That is the real spirit of the provisions of sub-rule (2) of rule 10 of Order 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

parties:
Bazlur Rahman and others.....Plaintiff-Petitioners
vs
Moniruampur Pourashava represented by its Chairman and others Defendant-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No.1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 17-4-2019 (decree signed on 24-4-2019) passed by the learned District Judge, Jashore in Title Appeal No. 90 of 2016 affirming those dated 28-6-2016 (decree signed on 30-6-2016) passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Monirampur, Jashore in Title Suit No. 178 of 2000 should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. Material facts of the case, briefly, are that the predecessor of the petitioners as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 178 of 2000 in the Court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Monirampur, Jashore impleading the opposite parties as defendants for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in respect of ka schedule land and recovery of khas possession in the kha schedule land. 

 3. The plaintiffs case in short is that the land measuring 28 (twenty eight) decimals in CS Plot No.210 of CS Khatian No.56 originally belonged to Tomizur Sardar, who gave settlement 1(one) decimal of land in CS Plot No.209 to Madan Bosk Kuchayan; that land measuring 49(forty nine) decimal under CS Plot No.208 of Khatian No.760 originally belonged to Tomiz Sardar. Madar Bosk kuchayan died without any issue and Tomiz Sardar took 2(two) decimals of land in CS Plot No.209 in his khas possession; that the three suit plots are situated in a compact block and adjacent to one another; that Tomiz Sarder died leaving only son plaintiff. Monirampur Union Parishad No.5 had no land or building of its own and the plaintiff for the welfare of the local people allowed the Union Parishad to use his land for temporary basis as its office on condition that the title of the suit land will remain in favour of the plaintiff and the plaintiff will pay all rents and other taxes for the land and in future if the office of Union Parishad is shifted otherwise, the suit land would be vested to the legal heirs of plaintiff and accordingly, plaintiff on 18-6-1960 executed and registered a "Nirupon deed" in favour of the then chairman of local Union Parishad and the Union Parishad started to run it's function by constructing one storied building on the said land and thereafter, some part of mouza within Monirampur Union and other two Unions declared as Pourashava and Monirampur Union Parishad shifted its office and started its functions on the land situated within Durgapur Mowza and thereupon, the effectiveness of the deed dated 18-6-1960 has been abandoned and the suit land was vested to the plaintiff and plaintiff got possession of the suit land on 15-1-2000; that Nazrul Islam ex-chairman of the then Union Parishad executed and registered a kabala deed in favour of the Pourashava illegally and Pourashava on 15-2-2000 demanded the suit land and dispossessed the plaintiff forcibly and on 1-6-2000 plaintiff asked the chairman of the Pourashava to vacate the suit land in favour of the plaintiff and Chairman refused to do so and claimed title of the land in question on behalf of Pourashava and hence, the suit. 

 7. Against which the heirs of the original plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 90 of 2016 before the learned District Judge, Jashore who by the impugned judgment and decree dated 17-4-2019 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree dated 28-6-2016 passed by the trial Court below. 

 10. Mr Rafiqul Islam Sarder further submits that the intention of the sole original plaintiff, Golam Mohammad Sarder (predecessor of the present plaintiff-petitioners) to establish office on his land for an unlimited period only for the purpose of local Union Parishad office and when local Union Parishad office will be established otherwise his land would be returned back automatically as per deed dated 18-6-1960 (Exhibit 3) and it is on record that the Union Parishad office has been terminated otherwise and the local Union Parishad chairman beyond any law most illegally executed a deed in favour of the Pourashava as to the suit land although both the Courts below having failed to consider this vital aspects of the case from a correct angle and whereby mechanically dismissed the suit on erroneous findings which resulted in the failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that original plaintiff, Md Golam Rahman by deed dated 18-6-1960 gave permission to the then Union Parishad to use his land until the local Union Parishad office is shifted otherwise and admittedly the office of the Union Parishad has been shifted to Dabidapur and by the deed dated 18-6-60 actual title of suit land has not been transferred in favour of the Union Parishad and both the Courts below ought to have considered that by the deed dated 18-6-19960 the Union Parishad did not acquire any title over the suit land and the Union Parishad had no right to transfer the suit land and therefore, by the deed dated 19-1-1998 and 16-2-1998 the defendant No.1 did not acquire any title since both the deeds were executed and registered by unauthorized persons and the Courts below in failing to do so committed an error of law resulting in an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate to strengthen his submission has relied on the decisions reported in 66 DLR (AD) 37 and 52 DLR (AD) 121. 

 11. Mr Ali Imam Khaled Rahim, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-opposite party No.1, on the other hand, opposes the Rule and supports the judgment and decree of both the Courts below, which were according to him just, correct and proper. The learned Advocate at the very outset submits that admittedly Paurashova has been constructed upto 2-storied building in the year 1981-1982 and from a plain reading of the impugned deed it is apparent that the sole plaintiff gave his land in favour of the local Union Parishad office and subsequently said local Union Parishad converted as local Pourashava named Monirampur Pourashava and thus in no way it cannot be said that the authority of the Union Parishad violated the terms and condition of the deed dated 18-6-19960 or the intention of the original plaintiff has been ignored. The learned Advocate further points out that according to deed dated 18-6-1960 (Exhibit 3) the original plaintiff should have been paid all rents of the suit land by his own money but the sole plaintiff in fact did not pay any rent as to the suit land and in this backdrop, the local Union Parishad office namely Monirampur Union Parishad mutated his name in the suit land and thereafter, paid rents to the Government since 1981 and thereafter, as per legal requirement of the Government for establishment of pourashava building the local Union Parishad chairman transmitted the land to the TNO by registered deed and in this way the Paurashava building has been constructed on the suit property and under the attending facts and circumstances of the case it does not lie in the mouth of the heirs of original plaintiff that since no Union Parishad office is there the land in question should be returned to them. Finally, the learned Advocate referring to section 60(b) of the Easements Act, 1882 submits that the licensee, acting upon the license has executed a work of a permanent character and incurred expenses in the execution and in this case the defendant opposite party No.1 admittedly constructed permanent character by expending its money it cannot be revoked and the plaintiffs in the attending facts and circumstances at best can claim money as compensation if they so advised and if it is open to them. 

 13. On scrutiny of the record, it appears that the sole plaintiff-petitioner filed Title Suit No. 178 of 2000 in the Court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Monirampur, Jashore praying the following reliefs: 

 14. It is found that at the trial both the parties led evidence to prove their respective case out of which the son of the original plaintiff was examined as PW 1, who stated in his deposition that—

VS
Md Abdul Hye and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
4. East Pakistan Government also made an order in 1966 under Rule 161 titled 'The East Pakistan Enemy Property (Lands and Building) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966'. 

 11. Although by the operation of the Proclamation of Independence and the Laws of Continuance Enforcement Order, 1971, the 1969 Ordinance lost its applicability in the People's Republic of Bangladesh, in 1974 the Government of Bangladesh, for ensuring further equality of all the citizens promulgated the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Act, 1974 (Act XLV of 1974), expressly repealing Ordinance I of 1969. However, the 1974 Act stopped short of return of the 'enemy property' to the original owners or their heirs who became citizens of Bangladesh and in fact the 1974 Act left all 'enemy properties' and firms which were vested with the custodian of 'enemy property' in the then East Pakistan, vested in the Government of Bangladesh. Pursuant to section 3 of the 1974 Act, such properties remained as vested on the Government of Bangladesh, however, the Act did not give any wide power of managing or disposing of such properties by the Government. 

 17. In 1999, the Parliamentary Standing Committee prepared a draft law with a view to return of possession of the properties listed as 'enemy property' since 1969 to their original owners who were a citizen of Bangladesh or their heirs under applicable personal law. The title of the draft law was Vested Property (Return of Possession) Bill, 1999. Pursuant to the draft law, it was expected that upon enactment, subject to the provision of determination claim provided in the draft Act, any property which was not listed prior to 16th February, 1969 would cease to be treated as vested on the Government as 'enemy property' and the title and possession of the original owner who is a citizen of Bangladesh or his lawful heirs would be restored. In the said draft of 1999, it was expressly provided upon enactment of the draft Act, any lease created by the Government on such properties would be deemed to be cancelled. 

 19. Thereafter, the Parliament enacted the 2001 Act clearly deviating from the initial scheme of reinstating title and possession of the original owners of the properties listed as enemy property, the 2001 Act, excluded a large number of properties from the list by operation of section 6 of the 2001 Act, which reads as follows: 

 h. The Government may take necessary measures by enacting law in respect of properties which were vested to the Government and where institution have already been developed for the purpose of the development of the country may be named after the name of the original and lawful owner; 

 "In England the Lewisham Union principle was given up as it would have the effect of allowing the public functionaries a free hand in ignoring their public duties. In countries like ours it will have a far more serious effect as many instances of non-performance of legal duty by Government and public functionaries will remain without remedy, thereby eroding the concept of rule of law and constitutionalism. This principle originated in England and when it has been discarded there, there is no rationale for insisting on the application of this principle in our country. It is submitted that the language of Article 102(2) leaves no scope for application of the Lewisham Union principle in our jurisdiction. Article 102(2) does not require that the applicant for mandamus must have a 'specific legal right'; the only requirement is that he must be an 'aggrieved party'. It is important to note that Article 31 provides a guarantee that no person in Bangladesh can be adversely affected except in accordance with law. Thus if a person is going to be affected by the failure of a public functionary to do what he is required by law to do, he can claim performance of the legal duty of the public functionary whether or not he has a specific legal right to claim performance of the duty. In Hazerullah vs Assistant Commissioner, Board of Management of Abandoned Property, relying on Lewisham Union, the Appellate Division held that a person can avail writ jurisdiction by way of mandamus only for enforcement of his legal right or for redress violation of such right. It is submitted that the Appellate Division was wrong in relying on 'Lewisham Union when it was discarded by the House of Lords in IRC vs Federation of Self-Employed; furthermore the finding is neither in conformity with the language of Article 102, nor comports with the finding of the court in Dr. Mohiuddin Farooque vs Bangladesh. Mandamus may issue where there is a violation of a legal right or violation of a legal duty." 

 Government may utilize the unclaimed vested property for the purpose of human development i.e. for betterment of the common people. Direction-(h), The Government may take necessary measures by enacting law in respect of properties which were vested to the Government and where institution have already been developed for the purpose of the development of the country may be named after the name of the original and lawful owner. 

 There is no statutory compulsion, on the part of the Government to enact a law in respect of properties which are vested to the Government and where institution have already been developed to be named after the name of the original owner.
